# ¶ Moral Exposition of the Romance of the Rose

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'S' featuring floral and foliate patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

Since it is true that things worthy of remembrance for their benefit and usefulness should endure forever, without being entirely lulled to sleep by the passing of many seasons and the fragility of fleeting and transitory time, the spur and stimulus of right reason and true cause have summoned and exhorted me—acting as the guardian of all that is good and honorable—to restore and return to its original state the book which, for a long time prior to this modern age, has been so highly esteemed by all intellectual folk that every person deigns to look upon it and keep it in the most prominent corner of their library, because of the sound maxims <note>original: "sentences," referring to pithy moral observations or judgments</note> and the natural and moral sayings and discourses contained and inserted therein. This is the pleasant book of the *Romance of the Rose* <note>original: "romant de la rose"</note>, which was poetically composed by two noble authors worthy of the esteem of all good sense and praiseworthy knowledge: Master Jean de Meun and Master Guillaume de Lorris. This present book has previously been, as I believe, poorly corrected due to the fault of the printers, or perhaps because of those who provided the manuscript <note>original: "le double," the copy provided to the printer</note> to be printed, for either one could be the cause of its errors <note>original: "incorrection"</note>. To restore this work to a better state and a more useful form for the understanding of readers and listeners, despite the weakness of my own small understanding...

<summary>This preface introduces a new, corrected edition of the Romance of the Rose, asserting that the work's moral value justifies its preservation despite previous printing errors.</summary>
<keywords>Romance of the Rose, Jean de Meun, Guillaume de Lorris, printing history, moral philosophy, literary restoration</keywords>

# THE PROLOGUE

[understand]ing and the unworthiness of my rustic wit <note>original: "rural engin," a modest self-deprecation common in the period, suggesting a lack of sophisticated education</note>, I have nonetheless desired to reread this present book from its beginning until its end. I have employed myself very laboriously in doing this, and have corrected it as best I could, adding references to the most important notable points and authorities <note>marginal citations of ancient or biblical authors</note> where they are relevant. I did this not purely of my own voluntary consent, as you should understand, but as I have said, at the instigation, prayer, and request of an honorable person, Galliot du Pré <note>A prominent Parisian bookseller and publisher active in the early 16th century, famous for his "Galley" trademark.</note>, a sworn merchant bookseller of the University of Paris. He has recently had it printed after seeing the state of it—both because of the bad and too-ancient language, which tastes of its antiquated beginning and origin of speech, and because of the imperfect quality of the verses, which were almost all corrupted.

And whereas some might say, as many have already said, that this book—by speaking in vain of the state of love—may be the cause of turning minds toward evil and applying them to dissolute things, because of the persuasive matter of foolish love <note>original: "fol amour," a literary term for obsessive, irrational, or purely physical passion</note> contained throughout its length; and because foolish sensual appetite, or sensuality (the nurse of all evil and stepmother of virtue), is the driver of its subject matter—with all honor saved and granted—I respond that the author’s intention is not simply, or in itself, ill-founded or evil. For it may well be that the said author did not cast his thought and imagination only upon the literal sense, but rather at[tended...]

# THE PROLOGUE

[granted <note>The text continues from the previous page's unfinished thought, likely "granting that he..."</note> that he] drew his spirit toward an allegorical and moral sense, as if saying one thing and understanding the other. I do not wish to affirm what I say as absolute fact, but it seems to me that he may have done so. And even if this author did not thus regulate his meaning or enter beneath the moral covering to penetrate to the marrow <note>The "marrow" (moelle) is a common medieval and Renaissance metaphor for the deep, essential truth hidden beneath the literal "husk" of a story.</note> of the new mystical sense, nonetheless one can interpret it morally and in various ways.

I say then, first of all, that by the rose which is so greatly desired by the Lover, we understand the state of wisdom—well and justly compared to the rose for the values, sweetnesses, and scents within it, which is very difficult to obtain because of the obstacles placed in the way, on which I do not wish to dwell at present. And in this manner of interpretation, the Rose shall be symbolized by the Golden Rose <note>original: "rose papalle," referring to the precious ornament of gold, musk, and balsam blessed by the Pope on the fourth Sunday of Lent to represent Christ and spiritual joy.</note>, which is composed of three things: namely gold, musk, and balsam. For true wisdom must be of gold, signifying the honor and reverence we owe to God the Creator; of musk, because of the fidelity and justice we must have toward our neighbor; and of balsam for ourselves, insofar as we must hold our souls dear and precious, like balsam, pure and more valuable than all things in the world.

Secondly, one can understand by the rose the state of grace, which is similarly difficult to obtain—not on the part of Him who gives it, for that is God the Almighty, but on the part of the sinner, who is always hindered and distanced from the Giver <term>collateur: The bestower or granter of a spiritual benefit or office.</term> thereof,

He compares this spiritual wisdom to the "Golden Rose" of the Pope, assigning moral meanings to its physical components of gold, musk, and balsam.</summary>

## THE PROLOGUE

This manner of spiritual rose, so fragrant and aromatic, we can liken to those roses by the power of which the great Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), the Roman author of the comedic and mystical novel *The Golden Ass*.</note> returned to his original form, as it is written in the book of *The Golden Ass* <note>original: *l'asne doré*</note>. This occurred when he found the garland of rosebush flowers hanging from the sistrum <note>original: *fistre*, a musical rattle used in ancient religious rites. While the author attributes this to Ceres, goddess of grain, in the original story by Apuleius, it is associated with the goddess Isis.</note> of Ceres, goddess of the grains. For just as the said Apuleius, who had been transformed into an ass, recovered his first form as a sensible and rational man, similarly the human sinner—who has been made and converted into a brute beast through his irrational resemblance to them—reclaims his original state of innocence through the grace of God conferred upon him when he finds the garland or crown of roses. This is to say: the state of Penitence, hanging from the sweet sistrum of Ceres, which represents the sweetness of divine mercy.

Thirdly, we can understand the Rose to be the glorious Virgin Mary, because of her goodness, sweetness, and perfections of grace, of which I shall remain silent for the present. And know that this virginal rose is not easy for heretics to obtain; it is as if "Evil-Tongue" <note>original: *malle bouche*, a primary antagonist in the *Romance of the Rose* who represents slander and prevents the Lover from reaching the Rose.</note> alone prevents them from approaching her goodness. For they have spoken ill of her, wishing to stain and disparage her natural honor by saying that one must not greet her or call her "Mother of Pity and Mercy." This is the white rose that we shall find planted in Jericho, as the wise man says: *like a rose-plant in Jericho.* <note>original: *quafi plantatio rofe in hierico*, a reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:14, often used in medieval liturgy to describe the Virgin Mary.</note>

Fourthly, we can by the rose understand the infinite sovereign good and the glory of eternal beatitude...

<summary>The author provides three further allegorical meanings for the Rose: a symbol of transformation from sin to innocence (via Apuleius), a symbol of the Virgin Mary, and a symbol of eternal divine glory.</summary>

## THE PROLOGUE

...from which, as true lovers of its sweetness and perpetual pleasantness, we may obtain [grace] by avoiding the vices that hinder us, and by having the help of the virtues that will introduce us into the orchard of infinite joy, all the way to the rosebush of all goodness and glory, which is the **beatific vision** <note>In theology, the "beatific vision" is the ultimate direct self-communication of God to the individual person, the highest aim of the soul.</note> of the essence of God. This rosebush can be represented not by the roses of **Paestum** in Italy <note>A Greek city in Italy famous among Roman poets like Virgil and Ovid for its "biferi" roses, which bloomed twice a year.</note>—which bloom only twice a year, which is not very frequent—but rather by the rose presented to the wise King **Solomon** by the noble **Queen of Sheba**, the Ethiopian. We read of this, and it appears in the book of her problems and the questions she asked him to test his **wisdom** <note>original: *sapience*</note>, by which she was so marveled that her senses failed her, as it is written in the Book of Kings. 

She took two roses, one of which came from a natural tree, and the other was produced by simulation; for she had made it sophistically <note>In this context, "sophistically" means with clever artifice or as a forgery intended to deceive.</note> and through art to look exactly like the natural rose, so subtly was it worked. "Behold," she said, "two roses present before your peaceful majesty; one is truly natural, but the other is not. Therefore tell me, Sire, which is the natural rose; show it to me with your finger." 

Solomon, seeing this, had several **honey bees** <note>original: *mouches a miel*, literally "honey flies."</note> brought, thinking and considering through the science he possessed of all natural things that the said bees, according to their nature, would go immediately to the natural rose and not to the sophisticated one; for such pleasant celestial little birds and...

## THE PROLOGUE

...[a] honey-making [bee] <note>The text here refers to a famous legend where Solomon, unable to tell the two roses apart by sight, observes a bee choosing the natural flower over the artificial one.</note> desires and longs for sweet flowers above all things. Therefore, he showed the queen the true rose, distinguishing it from the other which was made of scents imitating nature. This natural rose can thus signify the infinite good and true celestial glory, which is neither artificial <note>original: *sophistica*; in medieval rhetoric, this refers to something deceptive or a clever imitation</note> nor deceptive like the glory of the present world, which deceives us in that we believe it to be true, but it is not. 

Therefore, whoever would wish to interpret the **Romance of the Rose** <note>original: *Rommant de la rose*</note> in this way, I say that he would find great benefit, profit, and utility hidden beneath the bark of the text, which is not to be despised; for there is a double gain: recreation of the spirit and delectable pleasure regarding the literal sense, and utility regarding moral understanding. 

Fables are made and invented to be explained in a mystical sense, wherefore they should not be held in contempt. If the great eagle of whom **Ezekiel** spoke when he said:

> A great eagle with large wings, full of feathers and of many colors, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar <note>original: *Aquila grandis magnarum alarum plena plumis & varietate, venit ad libanum & tulit medullam cedri* (Ezekiel 17:3)</note>,

who had so far extended its flying plumage, had only stopped at the bark of the cedar when he flew to Mount **Lebanon**, he would not have found the marrow of the tree, but would have returned in vain and lost his flight. Similarly, if we did not dig deeper than the bark of the literal sense, we would have only the pleasure of fables and stories without obtaining the singular profit of the **spiritual marrow** <note>original: *mouelle neupmatiq̄*; "pneumatic" refers to the breath of the spirit</note>—that is to say, that which comes through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit regarding understanding...

<summary>The author concludes the Solomon allegory by explaining that just as the bee finds the true flower, the reader must look past the "literal bark" of stories like the Romance of the Rose to find "spiritual marrow." This justifies the use of secular fables for religious and moral education.</summary>
<keywords>allegory, literal vs. mystical sense, Romance of the Rose, Solomon, Ezekiel, spiritual marrow, fables</keywords>

<meta>Following the table of contents provided on the previous page, this folio marks the official beginning of the poem itself. The text introduces the central conceit of the work: the dream-vision as a vehicle for truth, rather than mere fantasy.</meta>

Leaf I
a i

# ¶ HERE IS THE ROMANCE
## OF THE ROSE
### Wherein the whole art of love is enclosed

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration contained within a rectangular frame featuring an inner oval border. The image depicts a man sleeping in a bed with high-hanging drapes. There are two candles or posts at the foot of the bed. This scene illustrates the "Dreamer" beginning his vision.</image-desc>

<margin>
Macrobius
on the
dream
of Scipio.
</margin>

Many people go about saying that dreams
Are nothing but fables and lies;
But one can dream such a dream
Which nevertheless is not lying,
But rather is afterwards quite apparent.
As a witness for this, I can find
Macrobius, a most reliable authority, <note>original: *acteur treaffable*; Macrobius was a 5th-century philosopher whose commentary on Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio* was the standard medieval textbook for understanding the prophetic and philosophical nature of dreams.</note>
Who did not consider dreams to be fables;
Instead, he wrote down the vision
Which happened to Scipio. <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, a Roman general. In the famous text by Cicero, Scipio has a dream where he is shown the celestial spheres and the immortality of the soul.</note>
Whoever believes or whoever says
That this is but a folly <term>musardie: a French term for idle distraction, daydreaming, or a foolish waste of time.</term>

<summary>This opening page of the Romance of the Rose establishes the poem's legitimacy by citing Macrobius and the Dream of Scipio to argue that dreams can contain profound truths. It sets the stage for the narrator's upcoming allegorical dream-vision.</summary>
<keywords>Macrobius, Scipio, dreams, vision, allegory, Romance of the Rose, prologue</keywords>

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the prologue from Leaf I, shifting from the philosophical defense of dreams (citing Macrobius) to the narrator’s personal experience. He introduces the specific dream that forms the narrative of the poem, dating it to his twentieth year.</meta>

# THE ROMANCE

Whoever wishes to hold me for a fool
For believing that any dream comes true,
May do so; but as for me, I have faith
That a dream is a signification <note>original: *signifiance*; a term from medieval semiotics meaning a sign that points to a deeper truth or a foreshadowing of future events.</note>
Of the blessings and the troubles that come to people;
The reason being, that at night one dreams
Of many things in a hidden way
Which one later sees quite clearly.

In the twentieth year of my life,
At the point when Love takes his toll <note>original: *prẽst le peage*; "taking the toll" refers to the inevitable moment in youth when one falls under the power of Desire, treated here like a tax or passage fee one must pay to enter adulthood.</note>
From young people, I went to lie down
One night, as was my custom,
And indeed, I fell fast asleep.
While sleeping, a dream occurred to me
Which was very beautiful to behold,
As you will hear me describe;
For in the seeing of it, it pleased me much,
And there was nothing in the dream
Which did not later happen in full,
Exactly as the dream recounted.
I wish to set this down in rhyme,
The better to lead you with pleasure;
Love requests and commands it of me.
And if, by chance, anyone asks
What I wish this romance
To be called, let the lover know
That it is the **Romance of the Rose**,
In which the whole **Art of Love** is enclosed.
The subject matter is beautiful and praiseworthy.

<summary>The narrator recounts a prophetic dream from his twentieth year, which he claims eventually came true in every detail. He identifies the poem as the "Romance of the Rose," a work commissioned by Love that contains the entire art of courtly affection.</summary>
<keywords>dream-vision, Love, the Rose, Art of Love, youth, prophecy, autobiography, Middle French literature</keywords>

--- Page 27 ---
<meta>This page continues from the prologue, where the author established his belief in the truth of dreams. Having dated the dream to his twentieth year, he now dedicates the work to his lady and begins the vivid description of the dream’s springtime setting. The "five years and six months" mentioned suggests the narrator is now roughly twenty-five years old as he composes this account.</meta>

# OF THE ROSE

May God grant that it be pleasing
To her for whom I have undertaken this;
She is a lady of high worth,
Who is so worthy of being loved
That she should be called "Rose."

<margin>Description of the summertime</margin>
It seemed to me at that time—
Quite five years and six months ago—
That I was dreaming in the month of May,
In the season of love, free from sorrow, <note>original: *sans esmoy*; literally "without dismay" or "without trouble," reflecting the ideal state of the courtly lover in spring.</note>
The time when everything laughs and rejoices,
When one sees neither bush nor hedge
That does not wish to adorn itself in May
And cover itself with new leaves.
The woods recover their greenery,
Which are dry as long as winter lasts;
The earth itself feels proud
Because of the dew that descends,
And forgets the poverty
In which it lived all winter.
Indeed, it finds itself so cheerful
That it wants to have a new dress;
And it knows how to make such an elegant <note>original: *coincte*; meaning clever, quaint, or skillfully fashioned.</note> dress
That it has many pairs of colors.
Of herbs and flowers, red and bluish-purple, <note>original: *perses*; a specific medieval term for a deep, indigo-like blue or bluish-purple fabric or color.</note>
And of many diverse colors
Is the dress that I describe,
By which the earth prizes itself more.
The little birds, who kept silent
While the great frosts were upon them,

<sig>a ij</sig>

<summary>The narrator dedicates his work to a lady he calls "The Rose" and describes the beginning of his dream, which takes place in a vibrant, personified May landscape. The earth is depicted as shedding its winter "poverty" to don a colorful, flowered garment.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, allegory of the Rose, May, springtime, personification of Nature, courtly love, medieval color theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the description of the arrival of spring. The narrator has just described the earth putting on its "new dress" of flowers and the birds beginning to sing again after the winter frosts.</meta>

# THE ROMANCE

Because the harsh and harmful weather has passed,
They are so at ease in the peaceful time
Of May that they show through their singing
<margin>Note on the nightingale</margin> That there is so much joy in their hearts
That they are compelled to sing by force.
The nightingale then exerts itself
To sing, making a sweet melody;
Then the parrot and the lark
Exert themselves and burst into song. <note>original: *se degoyse*; meaning to sing in a varied, chirping, or joyful manner.</note>
Thus it behooves young people to intend
To be merry and amorous
Because of the beautiful, vigorous springtime.
Hard-hearted is he who does not love with noble love <note>original: *amour franche*; referring to "sincere" or "noble" courtly love, a central theme of the poem.</note>
When he hears the birds on the branch
Singing their graceful songs
In that delightful season
When every living thing rejoices in loving.
One night while I was dreaming,
It seemed to me, as I slept soundly,
That it was truly morning.
I rose quickly from my bed,
Dressed myself, and washed my hands.
I took a silver needle
From a dainty and elegant needle-case, <note>original: *aiguillier*; a small case for holding needles, often a decorative personal item in the Middle Ages.</note>
And wishing to thread the needle,
I had a desire to go out of the city
To hear the songs of the birds
Who were now singing among the bushes.
In that new season,
Sewing my sleeves with a lace stitch, <note>original: *a videlle*; a technique of decorative lacing or stitching used to fasten sleeves, which were often separate pieces of clothing in medieval fashion.</note>

<summary>The narrator describes how the joy of spring compels birds and young people alike toward love. He then begins the action of his dream, rising early in the morning to leave the city and enjoy the birdsong.</summary>
<keywords>nightingale, parrot, lark, springtime, courtly love, silver needle, medieval fashion, dreaming</keywords>

->### OF THE ROSE<-

a iiij

<meta>The text is printed in an early Roman typeface. The initial letter 'M' is a large ornamental capital spanning two lines. There is slight ink bleed-through from the reverse side of the page.</meta>

I went along all alone, enjoying myself,
And listening to the little birds
Who were striving to sing well
Among the gardens that were blooming,
Pretty and gay, full of joy.
I headed toward a river <note>original: *madreſſe* (m'adressai); the narrator directs his steps toward the sound of the water.</note>
Which I heard babbling nearby;
For I never saw a more beautiful place
To take my pleasure <note>original: *me deduyre*; a common medieval term for seeking refined amusement, delight, or courtly leisure.</note>
Than along this river.
From a small hill just behind it,
The water descended, running swift,
Fresh, noisy, and as cold
As a well or a spring;
It was not as deep as the Seine, <note>A comparison to the river in Paris, suggesting the narrator's familiarity with the city.</note>
But it was more spread out.
Never had I seen or heard of
Such water as this which flowed,
And so my eye was never sated
With looking at the pleasant site
Of this clear and shining water.
Then I washed my face,
And saw well-covered and paved
All the bottom of the water with gravel;
And the meadow, large and beautiful,
Reached to the foot of this hill.
Clear, serene, and beautiful was
The morning, and temperate;
Then I went through the meadow,
Wandering all downstream,
Following this beautiful riverbank.

<summary>The narrator wanders alone through blooming gardens toward a clear, swift-running river. After washing his face in the cold water, he admires the gravel-bottomed stream and the serene morning air as he walks along the bank.</summary>
<keywords>Roman de la Rose, Guillaume de Lorris, dream vision, spring landscape, river description, courtly leisure, nature, meadow</keywords>

### THE ROMANCE

s. ii

When I had gone a little further,
I saw an orchard, long and broad,
Enclosed by a high wall, richly
And vividly carved on the outside
With many fine sculptures.
I gazed everywhere at the images
And the paintings upon the wall;
Therefore, I will gladly tell you
Of their form and appearance,
Just as I remember them.

->¶ Hate.<-

<margin>Description of Hate</margin>
In the middle appeared Hate,
Who, through false reports and through ire,
Seemed indeed to be a troublemaker <note>original: *mouveresse*; a person who stirs up or instigates strife.</note>
And a quarreler in brawls as well.
And this image truly resembled
A woman of very evil spirit.
She was not well adorned in her dress,
Nor was she orderly in her attire;
Her face was all wrinkled,
Her nose broad, and her eyes sunken.
She was withered and grimy, <note>original: *enroillée*; literally "rusty," used here to describe a complexion or appearance that is dark, dirty, or encrusted.</note>
And about her head she was
Hideously wrapped in a cloth
Of a very foul and wretched cut.

<meta>catchword: ¶ Felony.</meta>

<summary>The narrator discovers a vast orchard enclosed by a high wall decorated with vivid sculptures and paintings. He begins to describe these allegorical figures, starting with Hate, who is depicted as a repulsive, shabbily dressed, and angry woman.</summary>

### XI

### OF THE ROSE

The place was neither prideful nor stingy <note>original: "Neſtoit ne deſdaigneulx ne chiche." The narrator personifies the garden as being generous and welcoming in spirit, unlike the vices painted on the outside.</note>,

All placed themselves in her power <note>original: "dangier." In medieval literature, "dangier" refers to the power, control, or jurisdiction one person has over another, often used in the context of a lord or a lady in love.</note>

It would be a great burden for me
To declare them all to you by number,
But know that the trees were
Spaced apart as they ought to be;
One was set from the other
By five or even six **toises** <term>toise: a medieval French unit of length, roughly equivalent to 6.4 feet or 1.9 meters.</term>.
But they were very leafy and tall
To keep out the heat of summer;
So thick were they at the top
That the heat could not pierce them,
Nor could it descend to the bottom
To do harm to the tender grass.

In the **orchard** <note>original: "verger." In medieval literature, the *verger* or *locus amoenus* (pleasant place) was a standardized setting for courtly love and visions.</note> are fallow deer and roe deer,

In beautiful and lovely ways.

Had established there by conduit;
The water flowed down, making
A sound, melodious and pleasant.
At the edges of the streams and banks,
The grass grew thick and lush
In beautiful, lovely ways.

## OF THE ROSE

So that the joy may remain with you,

It would soon be wasted.

<margin>It is a great hardship to love.</margin>

¶ Love speaks to the lover

“Fair friend, by my father’s soul,
No one possesses a good thing if he does not pay for it.
One loves an acquisition much more
When one has bought it very dearly;
And those benefits are received with greater gratitude
Which one has obtained through hardships,
Than those which one had for nothing,
For those are too often held in low esteem. <note>original: "violant"; in this context, it suggests treating something with lack of respect or undervaluing it because it was too easy to obtain.</note>
There is no man who truly knows the pain
That the lover suffers, and the anguish;
No one could fully describe the ill of loving—
Even if he were to empty the sea—
By recounting it in a romance <note>original: "rommant"; referring to a narrative poem written in the vernacular (Old French) rather than Latin.</note> or in a book.
And nonetheless, it is necessary to live;
For lovers, this is their trade; <note>original: "mestier"; meaning a profession, craft, or necessary way of life.</note>
Each one flees the path of death.
The man who is put in a dark dungeon,
Amidst vermin and filth,
Who has neither barley bread nor oat bread,
Does not die from his hardship;
Hope <note>Hope (Esperance) is personified here as a divine or allegorical force that sustains the lover through the "pains of love."</note> delivers comfort to him,
So that he expects to find himself set free
Yet by some remedy or means. <note>original: "cheuissance"; a term for a resource, a way out, or a financial/legal remedy.</note>
Just so, and in such a balance,
He whom Love holds in prison
Fully expects to find a cure.” <note>original: "garison"; meaning healing, recovery, or the ultimate "salvation" of the lady’s favor.</note>

<margin>The third good: Sweet Sight.</margin>
The third benefit comes from looking;
It is **Sweet Sight** <note>original: "doulx regart"; also translated as Sweet Glance or Sweet Look. In the poem, these are personified comforts granted by the God of Love.</note> who knows how to wait
For those who have distant loves <note>original: "amours loingtaines"; a reference to the courtly ideal of "amor de lonh," or love from afar, where the beloved is physically distant or unattainable.</note>.
For this reason, I tell you to keep yourself

For which they are so curious;
For on the day they are able to see it,
No misfortune should befall them.
<margin>The consolation of Sweet Sight.</margin>
Such a man fears neither rain nor wind
Nor any other living thing.
And when the eyes have their delights,
They are so learned and so accustomed <note>original: "duys"; meaning trained or habituated, as a hawk is trained for the hunt.</note>
That they alone now wish to possess joy;
Whereby the heart must rejoice,
For they cause the pains to be eased.
They act like a true messenger,
Which quickly sends word to the heart

# OF THE ROSE

Immediately after Love had spoken to me,
His pleasure was not contradicted.
But when he had vanished,
Then I was quite dismayed,
For I saw no one near me;
Thus I grieved for my wounds,
Knowing that I could not be healed
Except by the **bud** <note>original: "bouton"; the rosebud, which represents the youth and beauty of the object of his affection.</note> where I had
Set all my heart and all my intent;
And I had trust in no one else
Save in the God of Love to obtain it,
For I knew well for a truth
That I would have no chance of getting it
Unless his love intervened.
The rosebushes were enclosed
By a **fence** <term>fence: "claye"; a wattle-work or hurdle enclosure used to protect gardens in the Middle Ages.</term> all around, as they should be,
But I would have passed that enclosure
Most willingly for the sake
Of the bud, which smelled like balm,
If I had not feared anger or blame.
But it might have seemed to some
That I wished to **steal** the roses,
Which I would never think of,
Nor ever do on any day.

# THE ROMANCE

Before the thing is done,
There are a hundred places to retreat.
You have much to do with wicked people;
Consider which is more noble:
<margin>Reason's teaching to the Lover.</margin> Either to leave off or to pursue
That which makes you live in sorrow.
It is the sickness named Love,
In which there is nothing but evil without renown.
Everyone must believe it is folly,
For he who loves cannot do well,
Nor achieve noble conduct <note>original: "vasselage"; referring to the qualities of a worthy knight or vassal, implying that love makes a man weak and un-chivalrous.</note>.
<margin>Love is nothing but lost time and wealth.</margin> If he is a scholar, he loses his learning;
And then, if he practices another trade,
He will hardly be able to profit from it.
Thus, he has more pain
Than any hermit or white monk <note>A "white monk" refers to a Cistercian, known for their particularly strict and austere way of life. Reason argues that love is a more grueling "religion" than the harshest monastery.</note>.
The pain of it is immeasurable,
And the joy is of short duration.
Whoever has joy, it lasts very little,
And obtaining it is a matter of chance;
For I see many who labor,
Who in the end fail completely.
You never listened to my counsel
When you surrendered yourself to the God of Love.
Your heart, which is too flighty,
Made you undertake such an outrage <note>original: "oultraige"; in this context, it refers to an act of excess or a lack of restraint that goes beyond the bounds of reason.</note>.
<margin>Note</margin> A folly is quickly begun,
But the difficulty <note>original: "mesprise"; literally a mistake or a difficult undertaking.</note> lies in escaping it.
But put Love into indifference <term>nonchalloir: a state of being "cool" or indifferent; the act of casting off all concern for something that was previously consuming.</term>,
Which can only harm you and be of no value.

<summary>Reason delivers a stern lecture to the Lover, arguing that love is a ruinous pursuit that wastes time, destroys careers, and offers more suffering than the strictest religious life. ### To Reason, who finds fault with Love.

### ¶ Generosity to Resistance.

Have you declared war against him,

And is, moreover, one of your subjects?

That it drew all the pain out of it
And sweetened the pain of loving,
Which for a long time had seemed bitter to me.
I was never so very much at ease;
Well is he healed who kisses such a flower,
Which is so sweet and fragrant.
<margin>The kissing of the rose</margin>
I shall never be so sorrowful
That, if I remember it, I would not be
Full of solace and of joy.
But nonetheless, I have suffered many troubles
And many bad nights
Since I had kissed the rose;
The sea is not so calm
That it is not troubled by a little wind:
Loves <note>original: "Amours"; the plural suggests the various experiences, states, or personified aspects of love.</note> change so often.

**NOW** it is time that I tell you
How I was led to shame,
By which I was later much distressed,
And how the wall was raised,
And the castle, powerful and strong.

<summary>The Lover describes the ecstatic joy and healing power of kissing the Rose, made possible by Venus’s intervention. He showed me courtesy, indeed—
So great that no one could believe it—
When he permitted me to cross
The hedge and kiss the Rose.
I must not feel ill-will toward him;
I would be acting against my duty.
Alas! Against the God of Love
I shall make no more complaints or outcries,
Nor against Lady Idleness <note>original: "dame oyseuse" — the personification of leisure who first admitted the Lover into the Garden of Pleasure.</note> either,
Who has been so gracious to me.
I will do so no more, for I would be in the wrong
If I complained of the kindness they showed me.
Therefore, it is better for me to suffer,
And offer my body to martyrdom,
And wait in good hope
Until Love sends me relief.
<margin>Note</margin> It is fitting that I wait for mercy,
For he told me—and I remember it well:
"I will accept your service with favor,
And I will raise you to a high degree,
Unless wickedness takes it from you;
But do not expect hope <note>original: "espoir"</note> to come to you quickly:
Great good does not come in a short time."

<summary>The Lover resolves his internal conflict, deciding to remain loyal to the God of Love and Fair Welcome despite his current suffering. He concludes that great rewards in love require patience and the endurance of hardship.</summary>

It is disloyal loyalty

A despaired hope.

A reasonable madness.

<margin>Note</margin>

It is a health that is entirely sickly;

It is the thirst that is always drunk,
A drunkenness that gets drunk on thirst.
<margin>The good epithets of love</margin> <note>original: "epithetos damours"; an epithet is a descriptive term. Reason is providing a list of titles or names that define the nature of Love.</note>

A sweet ill, a malicious sweetness,

A sin stained with pardon,

It is a piteous cruelty;
It is the game that is never stable,
A state unstable and too changeable;
A strength too enclosed and yet strong,
Which moves everything by its efforts;
It is foolish sense, it is wise folly,
A prosperity both sad and merry.

If love does not join and bind them together;
It is my opinion, and it seems true to me,
That faith or hope are worth very little,
Nor justice, fortitude, or temperance <note>These are the three Theological Virtues (Faith, Hope, Charity/Love) and the four Cardinal Virtues (Justice, Fortitude, Temperance, Prudence). The poet argues that without Love, the others are hollow.</note>,
To him who has not true love with him.
The Apostle <note>original: "Lapostre"; referring to Saint Paul, specifically his discourse on Charity in 1 Corinthians 13.</note> says, and I believe it,
That alms-giving or martyrdom,
Nor any good thing that one might speak of,
Is worth nothing if love is lacking;
Without love, all things fail.
Without love, no man is perfect,
Neither in word nor in deed;
This is the end, this is the sum:
Love indeed makes the perfect man.
Love begins and completes the total;
Without love, man is not truly made.
Love unlocks those bound in iron; <note>Love is presented here as a liberating force that can free both spiritual and physical captives.</note>
Love has no care for war.
True love, which never ceases,
Delivers them to God, joins them to God.
Loyal love does violence to God <note>original: "fait a dieu force"; this suggests a mystical concept where the intensity of a soul's love "compels" or "overpowers" Divine justice with mercy.</note>,
For love strives to love Him.
When love weeps perfectly,
A very great sorrow comes to it then,
And true love is intoxicated by loving,
For great sorrow intoxicates love;
Then it must perforce sleep,
When in sleep it strives to love.

<summary>This page defines Love (Charity) as the essential virtue that gives meaning to all other spiritual qualities and religious acts, citing Saint Paul’s teachings. It concludes by describing the mystical, almost intoxicating sorrow and devotion of a soul striving to love God perfectly.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of divine Love (Caritas). Having established that Love is the foundation of all virtues and the force that binds the soul to God, the text now describes the mystical progression of the soul—moving from active meditation to passive contemplation—and focuses specifically on the Virgin Mary as the ultimate object of this holy affection.</meta>

-># THE ROMANCE<-

For love cannot be idle,
As long as it is healthy and alive;
Then it goes straight into meditation,
Then ascends into contemplation. <note>In medieval mysticism, these are two stages of prayer: "meditation" is the active use of thought and imagination to reflect on God, while "contemplation" is a higher, quiet state of direct spiritual looking or experiencing.</note>
There it rests and then awakens;
There it sees many a great marvel.
There it sees every good, there it sees everything to see;
There it finds all its knowledge.
There it sees all that can be seen;
There it feels all that can be had.
There it learns what can be learned;
There it takes of the good as much as can be taken.
But the more it takes and the more it learns,
The more the desire for it takes hold;
Its appetite always grows,
And it holds its longing keen. <note>original: "aces apetit"; suggesting that the closer the soul gets to the divine, the more its hunger for God increases rather than being satisfied.</note>
In love there is no clamor;
Everyone can love through love.
Since no one can bring an outcry against you for loving,
It behooves you to love by way of love.
With all your heart and all your soul,
I wish for you to love the sweet lady; <note>The "Sweet Lady" refers to the Virgin Mary.</note>
For she moves you to love her,
And through love she wishes to love you.
Love then the Virgin Mary;
Through love, join yourself to her. <note>original: "marie / marie"; the poet uses a pun here, rhyming the name of Mary with the verb "to marry" or "to join."</note>
Your soul wants no other husband;
In this way, be wedded to her.
After Jesus Christ, her spouse,
Give yourself to him, to him betroth yourself.

->### OF THE ROSE<-

Give and grant yourself to her,

¶ Of the other love I will tell the remedy,
According to the divine scripture,

When they know how to seek the means for it;
But I know well—not by divination—
How to continue the divine work. <note>original: "loeuure diuin"; here referring to procreation as a task mandated by God to maintain the world.</note>
With all their will and power should
Whoever lies with a woman
Take good care of their likeness, <note>That is, to ensure the creation of an heir or offspring similar to themselves.</note>
Because everything is corruptible, <note>Subject to decay and death.</note>

Nature wills that the sons emerge
To continue this work again,
So that by the one, the other is replaced.
Therefore Nature placed delight therein
For her pleasure, so she chose,
So that the workers would not cease
And would not leave this work behind;
For many would never take part in it
If they were not attracted by delight.
Thus Nature acted subtly;
Know that no one approaches it rightly,
Nor has a righteous intention,
Who covets it for delight alone;
For he who goes seeking only delight
Certainly makes himself and renders himself...

People are shocked and marvel

Seeing how they committed such deeds <note>original: "besongne"; literally "work" or "business," but here referring to the scandalous or reckless activities of their youth.</note>

# THE ROMANCE

A valiant man feels great shame <note>original: "vergongne"</note>
When he must ask for what he needs; <note>original: "sembe-songne"; literally 'his business' or 'his necessity.'</note>
he dwells on it much and worries greatly,
and suffers much before he finally begs.
He feels great shame in speaking his piece,
and also fears a refusal <note>original: "lescondit"; a rejection or denial of a request.</note>.
But when such a man has found someone
<margin>A friend is known in time of need.</margin> whom he has tested well,
so that he is certain of his love,
he goes to him to voice his complaints and cries
of every matter he dares to think,
without having shame of anything;
for how could he be ashamed,
if the other is such as I describe,
once he has told him his secret?

<summary>Reason describes the deep hesitation and shame a noble person feels when forced to ask for help, contrasting this with the total confidence and lack of shame one feels when confiding in a proven, loyal friend.</summary>

# OF THE ROSE

Never will a third person know of it,
And he will have no fear of being reproached,
For the wise man guards his tongue,
Which a fool could never do,
For no fool knows how to keep silent.
Such a good friend will help him
In every way that he can,
More joyful, in truth, to do this
Than the other is to receive it;
And even if he does not make his request,
He <note>Referring to the friend who is helping.</note> will feel no less distress
Than the one who asked it of him,
So great is the mastery <term>mastery: the absolute power or ruling influence</term> of love;
And he bears half of his grief,
Comforting him as much as he can,
And sharing in his joy,
If the love is shared as it should be.

<margin>The conditions of true friendship.</margin>

<margin>Note the saying of Cicero on friendship.</margin>
By the law of this friendship,
Tully <note>original: "Tulles"; referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman philosopher whose work "De Amicitia" (On Friendship) was a primary source for medieval ideas on the subject.</note> says in a writing of his
That we should indeed make requests
Of our friends that are honorable,
And we should grant their requests in turn
If they contain right and reason.
Otherwise, no request should be made,
Except in two cases that he excludes:
If someone wished to deliver him to death,
We must deliver him from it entirely;
If someone assaults his reputation <note>original: "renommee"; one's public standing or "fame," which was considered a vital asset in medieval society.</note>,
Let us ensure it is not defamed.

<summary>Reason explains that a true friend shares in both joy and sorrow without being asked, and invokes Cicero to define the ethical limits of friendship: one must only help in honorable matters, except to save a friend's life or reputation.</summary>
<keywords>Cicero, Tully, discretion, reputation, ethics of friendship, mutual aid, Roman de la Rose</keywords>

--- Page 218 ---
<meta>This page continues Reason's speech regarding the ethics of friendship, specifically concluding the reference to Cicero before transitioning into a critique of "feigned love" driven by greed rather than virtue.</meta>

# THE ROMANCE

In these two cases, one must defend them <note>Referring to a friend's life or reputation, as mentioned on the previous page.</note>
Without ever waiting for reason to intervene;
As much as love can offer an excuse,
A man must not refuse to do this.
This love that I propose to you
Is not contrary to my purpose.
This is the one I truly wish for you to follow,
And that you do not follow the other love at all.
One is devoted to every virtue,
But the other puts people to death.
Another kind of love I wish to describe to you,
<margin>Feigned love is to be blamed.</margin>
Which is the opposite of the good kind
And is almost entirely to be blamed.
It is a feigned <term>feigned: insincere or pretended</term> will to love
In a heart sick with the venom
Of great covetousness <note>original: "couuoytise"; an intense desire for wealth or the possessions of others.</note> and of gain.
This love is in such a precarious balance
That as soon as it loses the hope
Of the profit it wishes to attain,
It must fail and be extinguished;
For a heart cannot be a true lover
If it does not love people for themselves,
But instead pretends and goes about flattering them
For the profit that it expects from them.
That kind of love comes from Fortune <note>Fortune was often personified in medieval literature as a fickle goddess who controlled worldly wealth and status.</note>,
Which eclipses just like the moon
That covers and shadows the earth
When the brightness falls into its shadow,
And which has lost as much of its light
As it has lost its view of the sun.

<summary>Reason distinguishes between virtuous friendship and "feigned love" driven by greed, explaining that selfish affection vanishes as soon as there is no more profit to be gained. She uses the metaphor of a lunar eclipse to illustrate how this false love depends entirely on the "light" of external wealth.</summary>
<keywords>friendship, feigned love, greed, Fortune, virtue, lunar eclipse metaphor, Cicero</keywords>

And when she <note>The moon, personifying the fickle nature of love and Fortune.</note> has passed through the shadow,
She returns all illuminated
By the rays that the sun shows her,
Which shine against her from the other side.
This love is of such a nature
For it is soon bright and then obscure,
As soon as poverty clothes it
In its hideous and cloudy mantle.
And when riches shine upon it,
They lead it back all clearly;
It flees when riches fail,
And it fails as soon as they do.

<margin>
Note on
feigned
love.
</margin>

By the love that I name for you here,
Every rich man is well loved,
Even the avaricious man
Who does not wish to wash his vicious heart
Of the heat and of the vice
Of covetousness <note>original: "couuoytise"; the obsessive desire for worldly gain.</note> and avarice.
He is more "horned" than a branched stag,
The rich man who believes he is loved;
This is a great folly <term>folly: here used as "couardie," meaning a lack of noble sense or base behavior</term> for him.
It is quite certain that he loves no one;
How then does he think that he is loved?
He is a fool for this, and so he is called;
In this case, he is not wise at all.
He is like a great wild calf <note>A "wild calf" was a common medieval metaphor for someone who is unrefined, foolish, and lacks the capacity for intellectual or moral reasoning.</note>
Who understands neither rhyme nor reason,
At any time, hour, or season.
Certainly, that man is [only] lovable...

<margin>
In avarice,
there is little
love.
</margin>

<summary>Reason compares mercenary love to the moon, which only shines when the sun of wealth is present, and mocks rich men who are foolish enough to think people love them for anything other than their money.</summary>

<margin>Note.</margin>
Who desires a true friend,
If he does not love, I can prove it:
If he loves for wealth, then,
Since he is thus so covetous,
More than the suffering poor man.
The good man <note>The "good man" here is the virtuous individual who values people for their own sake rather than their utility.</note> gazes upon all his friends
And holds and keeps them before him,
And always proposes to keep them
Until his mouth is closed
And death comes to break him,
For he would sooner allow
His limbs to be parted from his body
Than he would suffer them to depart from him.
But would friendship begin
<margin>A man who does not love should not be loved.</margin>
In a heart that has no pity?
It is certain when one acts thus,
For everyone knows their own deeds.
Certainly, he should be much blamed,
<margin>Note.</margin>
The man who loves and is not loved. <note>In this context, Reason argues that if a man's "love" is actually greed, he cannot complain when he is not truly loved in return.</note>

<margin>Note on Fortune.</margin>
AND since we come to Fortune <note>Lady Fortune, a central medieval figure who controlled the "wheel" of fate, turning rich men into beggars and vice versa.</note>
And hold a sermon on her love,
I want to tell you of a proud marvel,
Such that you never heard the like.
I do not know if you will be able to believe it,
But nonetheless it is a true thing,
And one finds it written,
That it is worth more to people and profits them more—
<margin>Adverse Fortune</margin>
Adverse and contrary Fortune,
Than the sweet and the debonair one.

<meta>catchword: That</meta>

<summary>Reason argues that a true friend values loyalty unto death, while a man who "loves" only for wealth deserves no affection. She begins a paradoxical argument that misfortune (Adverse Fortune) is more beneficial than prosperity.</summary>

### OF THE ROSE

<margin>
Sometimes [adversity] is more profitable than prosperity.
</margin>
And if this seems doubtful, 
It is a very weak argument [to say] 
That the gentle and soft Fortune 
Lies to them, wounds them, and drives them mad. 
She suckles them like a mother, 
And does not seem to be bitter at all. 
She pretends to have a loyal heart 
While distributing her jewels to them, 
Such as coins and riches, 
Dignities and noble titles; 
And she promises them stability 
In a state of friendliness, 
And soon feeds them on vain glory 
Within worldly happiness. 

<margin>
The fickleness of Fortune.
</margin>
When she places them upon her wheel, <note>The "Wheel of Fortune" (Rota Fortunae) was a popular medieval concept. It depicted Lady Fortune spinning a wheel where those at the top are kings and those at the bottom are beggars, illustrating that worldly status is fleeting and unpredictable.</note> 
Each one believes himself to be such a great master, 
Seeing himself in such a high state 
That he could never fall from it. 
When she has placed them at such a point, 
<margin>
Note.
</margin>
She makes them believe they have so many friends 
That they do not know how to count them, 
And they cannot rid themselves of the crowds 
That come and go around them, 
Holding them as their lords. 
These friends promise to seek riches for them, 
Even to the point of giving up their own shirts— 
Indeed, even to the point of shedding their blood 
To protect and defend them, 
Ready to obey and follow them 
For all the days they have to live. <note>Reason is describing "fair-weather friends" who offer total devotion only as long as the person is high on Fortune's wheel.</note>

<term>Fortune</term>: The personification of luck or fate, often depicted as a fickle woman.
<term>Riches</term>: Material wealth, which Reason views as a distraction from true virtue.
<term>Amis</term>: Friends; specifically here, the false friends who disappear when wealth does.
<term>Gloire vaine</term>: Vain glory; the empty pride one feels from temporary worldly success.
<term>Roe de fortune</term>: The Wheel of Fortune.

<summary>Reason explains how Prosperity (gentle Fortune) deceives people by surrounding them with false friends and a sense of permanent security. She argues that this "vain glory" is a lie, as the Wheel of Fortune will inevitably turn.</summary>

# LE ROMMANT

And those who hear such words
Glorify themselves and believe them
As if it were the Gospel; <note>original: "euangille." The speaker uses a religious comparison to show how blindly people trust the flattery they receive when they are rich.</note>
And it is all useless flattery,
As they would well know afterward
<margin>Few friends are found in adversity.</margin>
If they had lost all their goods
And had no means to recover them.
Then you would see "friends" at work,
For out of a hundred apparent friends—
Be they companions or kinsmen—
If even one of them were to remain with them,
They ought to truly adore God for it.

<margin>Note on adverse fortune.</margin>
¶ This [prosperous] fortune of which I spoke,
When she dwells with men,
She troubles their understanding
And nourishes them in ignorance;
But the contrary and perverse [fortune],
When she overturns them from their high status,
Tumbling them around her wheel <note>The "Wheel of Fortune" (Rota Fortunae) is a recurring medieval theme: the same wheel that lifts a beggar to a king eventually turns to cast the king into the mud.</note>
Until she puts them face-down in the mud,
And sits upon them like a harsh stepmother, <note>original: "marastre." In medieval literature, the stepmother was a common trope for a cruel or unfeeling figure, contrasting with the "motherly" facade of Prosperous Fortune.</note>
Placing a painful plaster <note>A medicinal bandage or poultice.</note> upon the heart—
Dipped not in sour wine,
But in weary and meager poverty—
She shows very clearly that she is true [honest],
And that no one should trust
In the blessings of Fortune,
For there is no security there.
She [Adversity] makes them know and understand [the truth]
As soon as they have lost their wealth.

<summary>Reason argues that while success blinds people with flattery, misfortune is a "true" teacher because it reveals which friends are loyal and proves that worldly status is fleeting.</summary>

.XCVI
### THE ROMANCE OF THE ROSE

This [false] love was held by those
Who were their friends before;
For those to whom Prosperity <term>bieneurté: a state of worldly success, happiness, and wealth</term> gives gifts,
Misfortune <term>maleurté: the state of adversity or bad luck</term> greatly astonishes them.
And they [the false friends] become like enemies;
Not one remains, nor even half a one,
But they flee and renounce them
As soon as they see them become poor.
And yet they do not stop there,
But in every place they go,
They go about blaming and defaming them,
And calling them "miserable fools."
<margin>Note</margin>
Even those for whom they did the most good,
When they saw them in their high positions,
Go testifying with a cheerful voice
That their folly was well-deserved; <note>The text suggests that false friends justify their abandonment by claiming the victim's downfall was their own fault or "folly."</note>
Such people find no one to help them.
But the true friend remains,
Who loves not for riches—
So full is his heart of nobility—
Nor for any benefit he expects.
Such a one helps and defends them,
<margin>He who loves well is slow to forget. <note>original: "Qui bien aime tard oublie." A common medieval proverb emphasizing that true affection is not easily erased by time or trouble.</note></margin>
For Fortune has no influence over him;
Loyal friends love forever.
Even if one were to draw a sword against a friend,
Such love would not be severed,
Except in these cases I wish to name:
It can be broken by pride, by anger,
By reproach, and by revealing
Secrets that ought to be kept hidden.

<summary>Reason explains that while false friends abandon and mock a person in poverty, a true friend’s loyalty is independent of Fortune and can only be broken by personal betrayals like pride or the revealing of secrets.</summary>
<keywords>friendship, Prosperity, Adversity, loyalty, betrayal, Fortune, proverbs</keywords>

### THE ROMANCE

And by the painful wound
Of venomous detraction <term>detraction: the act of slandering or belittling someone's reputation</term>
Friends [of the false sort] would flee at this step;
They would do nothing else to harm him,
But such people manage themselves quite well.
<margin>Note</margin>
If among them they find even one [true friend],
So vain is the love of the world,
Completely full of ingratitude.
And because no wealth
Compares to the value of a friend—
For [wealth] never rises so high
That the good of a friend does not surpass it—
A friend on the way is always worth more
Than coins in a belt. <note>original: "amy en voye / Que ne ſont deniers en courroye." A common medieval proverb suggesting that a helpful companion is more useful than money during a journey or in times of trouble.</note>
But wicked Fortune,
When she falls upon the living,
By her misfortune she makes them
See all things so very clearly
That she leads them to find such [true] friends
And to prove by experience
That they are worth more than any possession
That one could have in this world.
<margin>Adversity is often worth more than prosperity.</margin>
Therefore, adversity profits them
More than prosperity does;
For by the latter they have ignorance,
And by adversity, knowledge. <term>science: in this context, it refers to wisdom or the "science" of knowing the truth of one's circumstances</term>
And the poor man who proves it so,
Distinguishes the true friend from the false;
He knows and recognizes them well,
[Better than] when he was rich as he wished.

<summary>Reason argues that Adversity is more valuable than Prosperity because it provides the "science" of truth, revealing who one's true friends are once the "venom" of slander and poverty drives away the false ones.</summary>

### OF THE ROSE Leaf XCVII
n i

What would he have been willing to pay then,
If he knew then what he knows now?
Certainly, he would have been much less deceived,
And would have been aware of it from that moment.
Thus, he has a greater advantage—
Since from a single [loss] he has become a wise man—
Through the great poverty that unmasks him,
Than from the wealth that receives him. <note>original: "La grant pourete quil decoit / Que richesse qui le recoit." Here, Reason suggests that poverty "deceives" the world's expectations but reveals the truth, whereas wealth hides it.</note>
For wealth does not make rich
The one who hides it away in a treasury;
But sufficiency <term>suffisance: the state of having "enough"; a key medieval virtue where contentment is valued over material abundance</term> alone
Allows a man to live richly.
For such a man may not have the value of a crumb, <term>miche: a small loaf or crumb of bread</term>
Who is more at ease and much richer
Than one who has a hundred measures <term>muid: a large medieval unit of capacity for grain</term> of wheat.
I can certainly tell you how this is:
For hope is his merchant,
And his heart is so wretched
That he is quite needy
Even before his goods are gathered;
Nor does he cease to worry
About increasing and multiplying,
And he will never have enough,
No matter how much he knows how to acquire.
But the other, who puts no trust
In material goods throughout his life,
But for whom what he earns is enough
When he can live by his own labor,
Does not believe that he lacks anything,
Even if he possesses not the value of a half-penny. <term>maille: a small coin of very low value, often a half-denier</term>

<margin>
**Note**
Sufficiency makes a man rich.
</margin>

<margin>
The rich man is insatiable.
</margin>

<summary>Reason explains that true wealth is found in "suffisance" (contentment) rather than hoarded gold. She argues that the poor man who is satisfied with his labor is richer than the wealthy man whose greed makes him perpetually needy.</summary>

And if it happens that he is sick

# THE ROMANCE

All their earnings and their savings
And then they go to carry their burdens
By pleasure to enjoy themselves
And loyally they earn their livelihood,
For to steal and take by force they do not deign
Then they go to their barrel and drink
And live as they ought to live.

<margin>Sufficiency contenting wealth</margin>
¶ That man is rich in abundance
Who truly believes he has sufficiency <term>sufficiency: "suffisance" refers to the state of being satisfied with what one has; a central medieval virtue contrasting with the sin of greed.</term>
By this he is more righteous

Could never be rich.
But is always poor and needy,
So wretched and covetous is he.
Also it is true, whether it pleases you or not,
The merchant does not live at his ease,
For he puts his heart into such a war
That it always burns to acquire more.
And he will never have acquired enough;
He fears losing what he has already acquired,
And missing out on the remainder
Of which he does not yet see himself possessing.
For he has no desire for anything so much
As to acquire the estate of another.
Undertaken with marvelous pain,
For he wants to drink all the Seine <note>original: "toute la seine" — A metaphor for the river in Paris, used here to illustrate the impossibility of satisfying infinite greed; no matter how much a merchant "drinks" (acquires), the river of wealth remains full and he remains thirsty.</note>
Of which he will never be able to drink so much
That there will not always be more of it;
This is the distress, this is the burning...

<summary>Reason argues that true wealth comes from contentment (sufficiency) rather than material accumulation. The text sharply criticizes usurers and merchants, whose insatiable greed is compared to trying to drink the entire River Seine.</summary>

### ¶ The Lover to Reason.

¶ "O Lady, by the King of Angels, teach me then in your ways: which things shall be mine? And can I truly have anything as my own? This I wish to learn from you."

### ¶ Reason to the Lover.

¶ "Yes," responded Reason then, "but do not mean a field or a house, nor fine robes and ornaments, nor any earthly holdings, nor even your own limbs in any manner. You possess a far better and more precious thing: these are the goods of your own mind <note>original: "sens" — can mean reason, intellect, or the internal senses.</note>, of which you are certain and aware; for they will remain with you without ceasing, such that they can never leave you to provide their service to another.

These goods are yours by right of office; but of those others which are external <term>forains: things that are outside of or foreign to the soul or the self.</term>, you do not possess the value of even two dozen <note>original: "deux douzains" — a common medieval expression for something of very little value.</note>. Neither you nor any living man possesses the value of a chive <note>original: "vne cyue" — a green onion or chive, used as a metaphor for something worthless.</note> of them; for know that all your true possessions are enclosed within yourself."

<summary>In this passage, the Lover asks Reason what he can truly call his own if external wealth and power are illusions. Reason explains that only the "goods of the mind"—intellect and virtue—are permanent and personal, while all physical property and even one's body are external and transitory.</summary>

# THE ROMANCE

Do you not remember Horace <margin>The maxim of Horace.</margin>
Who had so much wisdom and courage?
Horace said—and he was no fool—
That when fools flee from a vice,
They turn instead to its opposite,
Which makes their situation no better.
I do not wish to forbid Love,
Nor that one should not apply themselves to it,
Except for that love which causes people harm.
Therefore, if I forbid drunkenness,
I do not wish to forbid drinking,
For such a command would not be worth a pear <note>original: "vne poire" — a common medieval idiom for something of no value.</note>.

People would surely consider me mad
If I were to command avarice in its place;
For both the one and the other are vices.
I do not make such arguments.

# THE ROMANCE

### OF THE ROSE

[...The love] that I have prepared for you to love.

<margin>
The love of animals through natural inclination, as well as that of men.
</margin>
There is another natural love
Which Nature created in animals,
By which they provide for <term>provide for</term> <note>original: "cheuissent" — to manage, care for, or successfully rear.</note> their young,
And nurse and nourish them.
Regarding the love I am describing here,
If you wish me to tell you
What its definition is:
It is a natural inclination
To want to preserve one’s own kind
Through proper intention,
Whether by the way of procreation
Or by the care of feeding.
To this love, both men and women
Are as ready as the beasts.
Such love, however much it benefits,
Has no praise, blame, nor merit.
They are not to be blamed or praised for it,
For Nature compels them to it.
But if they did not do so,
They would deserve to receive blame;
Just as when a man eats,
What praise is owed to him?
But if he refused to eat,
One would surely have to rebuke <term>rebuke</term> <note>original: "ledangier" — to find fault with, or to place in a position of reproach or danger.</note> him.
I know well that you do not care
For this love in any measure;
You have undertaken a much more foolish endeavor
In the love you have embraced.

<vocab>natural love, nature, beasts, procreation, nourishment, blame, praise</vocab>

<summary>Reason defines "natural love" as the instinctual drive for procreation and the rearing of offspring shared by humans and animals, noting that while it is necessary for survival, it holds no moral virtue because it is driven by nature rather than free will.</summary>

It is not at all right or reasonable
That she should have a house in paradise,
For she is not so blessed;
Instead, she has a most perilous house.

A rock sits in the sea,
Very deep in the middle of it,
Which thrusts itself high above the water,
Against which the sea roars and rages. <note>This "rock" is the dwelling of Fortune. In medieval allegory, a rock usually signifies stability, but here it is situated in a "perilous" sea, suggesting that any security Fortune offers is surrounded by danger.</note>

They who always fight against her,
And many times they strike there so much
That they bury it entirely in the sea.
Sometimes it strips itself bare
Of the water that wets it all over,
When the wave <term>floc</term> <note>Middle French for a wave or the surge of the tide.</note> pulls back,
At which it leaps into the air and turns;
But it retains no constant form,
Instead, it transmutes and transforms,
And now disguises and changes itself,
Always dressing in a strange form.
For when it thus appears in the air,
It makes little flowers <term>fleurettes</term> appear,
Like brightly shining stars,
And little green grasses.
When Zephyrus <note>The West Wind, traditionally the herald of spring and growth in classical and medieval poetry.</note> rides upon the sea;
And when the North Wind <term>bise</term> <note>A cold, dry wind from the north; in this context, it represents the sudden "winter" of misfortune that destroys beauty and prosperity.</note> blows again, he mows down
The little flowers and the greenery
With the sword of coldness,
So that the flower loses its place there.

<margin>
The wind Zephyrus makes [the flowers] come.
</margin>

# OF THE ROSE

It is now of the King of Sicily <note>Manfred (1232–1266), mentioned on the previous page.</note>
Just as the true God willed it,

King Charles took from him

In the first battle <note>The Battle of Benevento (1266), where Charles of Anjou defeated Manfred to claim the Sicilian throne.</note>
He attacked him to defeat him.
"Check and mate," he went to say to him,
Upon his spirited warhorse,
By the move of a good wandering pawn <note>original: "pennet." A pawn in chess. The poet uses chess terminology to describe tactical maneuvers on the battlefield.</note>
In the middle of his chessboard.
Of Conradin <note>original: "Courrardin." Conradin (1252–1268) was the young nephew of Manfred who attempted to reclaim the kingdom but was captured and executed.</note> I do not wish to speak—
His nephew, whose example is ready—
Whose head King Charles took
Despite the princes of Germany.

He [Charles] made die in his prison.
These two, like false young boys,

And knights to the fire,
And they fell away from the chessboard.
Such fear they had then of being captured
In the game they had undertaken.
But whoever looks at the truth,
They had no protection against being taken;
Since they fought without a king,
They feared no "check and mate." <note>The poet suggests that without a living King (Manfred), the remaining players were essentially already defeated, as a game of chess cannot be won or technically "mated" if the King is already gone from the board.</note>

Which had departed from God
And had undertaken the battle
Against the faith of **Holy Church**.
And if anyone had called "**check**" to them,
There was no one who could come to their rescue,
For the **Queen** <note>original: "fierte." From the Persian *ferz* (vizier), this was the medieval name for the chess piece that later became the Queen.</note> was entirely captured

Where the king lost like a fool:

r iij

Whoever receives life in this world,
There is none who does not drink from these two barrels.
It is an open tavern
Where **Fortune** is the tavern-keeper,
Who draws from them into pots and cups
To make <term>sops</term> <note>original: "souppes." Slices of bread soaked in wine or broth. Here, it metaphorically refers to how Fortune "flavors" every person's life with a mixture of fate.</note> for everyone.
She gives everyone to drink with her hands,
But to some more, and to others less.

<margin>
The tavern of **Jupiter**.
</margin>

There is no one who does not drink every day
From these barrels, whether a quart or a pint,
Or a <term>hogshead</term>, a <term>sester</term>, or a <term>half-pint</term> <note>original: "muy," "septier," or "chopine." These are medieval liquid measurements. The poet is emphasizing that Fortune dispenses fate in varying quantities.</note>,

For she pours out good or evil to each,
Just as she is both sweet and perverse.
Indeed, no one will ever be so joyful,
When he truly stops to consider it,
That he does not find, even in his greatest ease,
Something that displeases him.
Nor will he ever have so much misfortune,
When he truly stops to consider it,
That he does not find in his <term>distress</term> <note>original: "desconfort." A lack of hope or consolation.</note>
Something for his comfort,
Whether it be a thing already done or yet to be done—
If he only thought well on his own affairs—
Unless he falls into **despair**,
Which brings all sinners to ruin; <note>In medieval theology, despair (desperatio) was considered a grave sin because it represented a total rejection of God's mercy.</note>
And no one can offer counsel against it,
No matter how much deep wisdom he has in <term>learning</term> <note>original: "la lettre." Literally "the letter," referring to formal education, book-learning, or the study of scripture.</note>.

<summary>Reason explains that Fortune acts as a tavern-keeper for Jupiter, dispensing a mixture of good and bad fate to every person. She argues that no life is purely happy or purely miserable, and warns that only the sin of despair can truly destroy a person's ability to find comfort.</summary>

To correct and teach you,

And if you were unwilling to believe me,
With my good and true word,
I could, when the time was right,
Bring a complaint to the judge who would do me justice.

### OF THE ROSE

The fortress would be surrendered.
No gate would be held there,
For all would then let it be taken;
There is nothing that could defend them,
No one would dare utter a word.
The path is named "Giving Too Much."
<margin>Note on Foolish Generosity <note>original: *folle largesse* — a courtly vice involving reckless spending or over-extravagant gift-giving to win favor.</note>.</margin>
Foolish Generosity founded it,
Where many a lover has sunk.
I know the path well,
For I came from there just the day before yesterday,
And I have been a pilgrim there
For more than a winter and a summer.
If you take Generosity to the right,
Without turning to the left hand,
You will have, for more than a bowshot <note>original: *archeé* — the distance an arrow flies; a common medieval unit of measurement.</note>,
The path well-trodden and walked
Without wearing out your shoe at all.
You will see the wall crumble there,
And towers and turrets stagger,
No matter how strong or beautiful they may be,
And the gates will be opened by those within,
For the guards are as if dead.
<margin>A way to have the castle of love.</margin>
On that side, the castle is
So weak that a little cake <note>original: *gasteau* — a wafer or soft bread; used here to emphasize how easily the walls can be broken compared to even the softest food.</note>

Than those walls are to knock down;
By that way, it would be taken quickly.
It would not require so great an army
As King Charlemagne <note>The King of the Franks and Emperor of the Romans (c. 742–814), legendary for his massive military conquests.</note> gathered
When he wished to conquer Germany.

No one emerges from it, evening or morning,
Unless Poverty puts her hand upon them,
By whom one is distressed or brought to a halt.
Foolish Giving <note>original: *Folle largesse* — the personification of reckless spending or excessive generosity, often depicted as a lady who throws money away.</note> dwells within,

Everyone insults and defames her.

Everything I preach to you here,
I say from my own personal experience.
I know well what poverty amounts to,
through my own hardship and shame,
dear friend—more than you know,
for you have not suffered it so much.

<header>OF THE ROSE</header>

He who takes warning <term>takes warning: *se chastie* in Middle French means to correct oneself or learn a moral lesson from the mistakes of others.</term> from the example of others used to be called a worthy man and was loved by all his companions. And I, too, used to spend joyfully in all places and quite generously, as long as I was considered rich. But now I have become poor through my spending and foolish generosity <note>original: *folle largesse*. While "largesse" was a celebrated knightly virtue of open-handed giving, the Friend admits he practiced it to a "foolish" or ruinous degree.</note>, which has placed me in such distress that I struggle to have anything at all—neither drink nor food, nor warmth nor clothing. Poverty, which strips me of every good thing, makes me feel such anguish.

Now know, friend, that as soon as Fortune <note>Lady Fortune was a central figure in medieval philosophy, often depicted turning a wheel that randomly raises people to power or casts them into poverty.</note> had placed me in this state, I lost every one of my friends, except for one alone, I truly believe, who has remained with me. Fortune thus took them from me because of the poverty that took hold of me. She took them, by my faith—I do not lie—but she simply took back what was her own property. For I know well that if those friends had truly been mine, they would never have left me on her account. Therefore, she did no wrong toward me when she reclaimed her own things. They were hers indeed, though I knew nothing of it; for I had bought them so dearly with my heart, my body, and my wealth.

<margin>
In adversity,
there are 
no friends.
</margin>

For hypocrites always hate

To bear witness to a good life,
Fine gifts are held in high regard everywhere;
He who gives a fine gift is a worthy man <term>preudhoms: a man of integrity, chivalric honor, and high social standing</term>.
Gifts grant praise to the givers,
And they diminish the takers

What more should I tell you in short?
By gifts, both God and man were won over.

Companion, hear this lesson
That I advise and note for you;
Know that if you wish to do
What you have heard me describe,
The God of Love will never fail,
When he assails the strong castle <note>The "Fortress of Jealousy," the allegorical prison where the Rose is kept under guard by personifications like Danger, Shame, and Fear.</note>,

For he and the goddess Venus
Will fight the gatekeepers so much
That they will tear down the fortress,
And then you may pluck the rose;
It shall no longer be so tightly enclosed.
But when the thing has been acquired,
It requires great mastery <term>maistrise: the skill, art, or self-control required to maintain a conquest</term>
To guard it wisely,
If one wishes to enjoy it for a long time;
For the virtue <note>Original: "vertu." In this medieval context, it refers to the strength of character or the specific power/skill required for an action.</note> is no less
To keep something well than to take it.
For when things are acquired <margin>Note</margin>
And they are lost by some means...

She cares so little for her love that she desires nothing from her dear friend but all his coins and his spoils. But if a woman is of good character, with a loyal heart and a modest face, I shall tell you exactly what a courtly and noble youth <term>varlet: originally a young gentleman or squire, here referring to a suitor in the service of Love</term> must do if he wishes to devote himself entirely to her. Let him take care not to rely solely on his beauty or his physical form; it is only right that he should shape his mind <term>engin: a person's natural wit, talent, or ingenuity</term> with good manners, the arts, and the sciences. For anyone who truly understands the ends and outcomes of beauty would see clearly that it can be preserved for only a very short time—scarcely until evening <note>original: "vespree." A common medieval metaphor comparing the fleeting nature of youth to the short life of a flower before dusk.</note>, like the little flowers in the meadow; for beauty is of such a painful nature that the longer it lives, the more it decays.

## Pierced, broke, and tore her heart,

For it would be better that she were drowned—
That disloyal, renounced woman <note>The man is instructed to insult the other woman (the mistress) to prove his loyalty to his partner.</note>—
Than that she ever came to a place
Where she held him in such a state.
For if it happens that she tries to lead him,
He will not go as she leads him.
Then he must embrace her tightly,
<margin>Note</margin>
Kiss, flatter, and comfort <note>original: "soulasser" — to provide solace, relief, or physical pleasure.</note> her,
And cry for mercy for the misdeed,
Since it will never be done again;
For he has sincere repentance,
Ready to perform the penance
As she will know how to enjoin him,
Once she has granted him forgiveness.
Then let him perform the work of love <note>The text suggests that physical intimacy is the final step in securing a woman's forgiveness after a quarrel.</note>
If he wants her to grumble no longer.
Take care that you do not boast of her;
She could be grieved by it.
Indeed, many have boasted of many women,
Through false and feigned words,
Whose bodies they could not possess;
They wrongfully defamed their names.
But truly those have failing hearts
Who are neither courtly nor valiant.
<margin>Note</margin>
Boasting is a most base vice;
He who boasts is a fool and a simpleton <note>original: "nice" — in Middle French, this meant ignorant or foolish, derived from the Latin "nescius."</note>.
