### CLXXXVI
### OF THE ROSE
<sig>& n</sig>

For even if he had succeeded well,
He nonetheless ought to conceal it;
Love wishes to hide its jewels <note>original: "ioyaux" — here referring to the private pleasures or "treasures" of an intimate relationship.</note>
Except from loyal companions
Who wish to keep them quiet and hidden;
There, one may well reveal them.
<margin>Note on concealing one’s affairs in love well</margin>
And if she falls into sickness,
It is right, if he can, that he strives
To be very helpful to her,
In order to be more pleasing to her afterward.
Take good care that weariness does not seize him;
If her sickness lasts a long time,
Stay near her, remaining by her side,
Kissing her and weeping.
Such a man should make vows, if he is wise,
To go on many a distant pilgrimage <note>original: "pelerinaige" — the lover is advised to make public religious vows to show his devotion, hoping the display of piety and concern will move her.</note>,
Provided that she hears these vows.
Do not forbid her food <note>original: "viande" — in Middle French, this referred to food or sustenance in general, not specifically animal meat.</note>;
He should not offer her anything bitter,
Nor anything unless it is sweet and tender.
He should feign for her new dreams,
Stuffed with pleasant lies,
Saying that when he lies down in the evening,
All alone in his room and his bed,
That it seems to him while he slumbers—
<margin>Fiction and persuasion <note>original: "Fictio & persuasio"</note> used by lovers toward their lady-loves</margin>
For he sleeps little and wakes little—
That he had held her in his arms
All night long and all naked,
For solace and for merriment,
Finding her all healthy and all cured.

<summary>The "Friend" advises the lover on the necessity of discretion and provides tactical instructions on nursing a lady through illness to gain her favor. # THE ROMANCE
### OF THE ROSE

And by day, in delightful places,
He tells her such stories, or similar ones.

Now have I sung up to this point,
Through sickness and through health,
Of how one must serve the ladies
If one wishes to deserve their grace
And to continue in their love,
Which can so easily shift.
Who would not want to give great attention
To doing whatever they desire?
For no man will ever truly know a woman,
Nor will she ever have a heart so firm,
Nor be so loyal or of such good character,
That a man can ever be quite sure
Of holding onto her, no matter his effort,
Any more than if he held in the Seine <note>The River Seine in Paris, used here as a symbol of something vast and impossible to grasp.</note>
<margin>Note on the fickleness <note>original: "variete" — here meaning inconstancy or changeability.</note> of women</margin>
An eel by the tail,
Which has such power to wriggle
That it has soon escaped,
No matter how strongly he had grabbed it.
Is such a beast not far from being tamed,
When it is always so ready to flee?
She is of such diverse changeability
That no one should place their trust in her.
I do not say this for the good women
Who found their lives upon virtue,
Though I have yet to find any,
No matter how well I have tested them;
Even Solomon could not find one. <note>A reference to the biblical King Solomon who, in the Book of Ecclesiastes, famously laments that he found "one upright man among a thousand, but not one upright woman among them all." This reflects the common medieval trope of clerical misogyny.</note>

<summary>This passage uses the metaphor of a slippery eel to describe the perceived fickleness of women and claims that even the wise King Solomon could not find a truly virtuous woman.</summary>

<meta>The page number LXXXVIII is visible as a ghost/bleed-through from the verso side, appearing reversed at the top left of the text block.</meta>

Even if she is called ugly,
Swear that she is more beautiful than a fairy,
And do this so vividly

For each one thinks of herself—

Even if she is proven to be ugly,
[Say] that she is truly worthy of being loved.
Thus, to keep their lady-loves
Without criticizing their follies,
All must be diligent—
The handsome squires, the brave, and the noble.
Women care nothing for correction; <term>chasty: from the verb 'chastier,' meaning to reprimand, discipline, or reform behavior.</term>
Rather, they have their minds <term>engin: wit, ingenuity, or natural disposition.</term> so constructed
That it seems to them they have no need
To be taught their own business. <note>original: "mestier" — meaning a trade or craft; here it refers to their way of life or conduct.</note>
No person <note>original: "fil" literally 'son,' but used here as 'no soul' or 'no one.'</note> wants to displease them,
Nor deny what they wish to do.
Just as the cat knows by nature
The science of "surgery," <note>original: "cirurgure" — an archaic form of surgery. In medieval metaphor, this refers to a cat's natural, untaught instinct for hunting and "dissecting" mice.</note>
Nor can one be turned away from it

And was never put to school for it;
Thus does a woman, so foolish is she,
By her natural judgment,
In all that she does excessively—
Whether it be good or bad, wrong or right,
Or whatever else you might wish—
[Believe] that she does nothing she ought not to do,
And she hates whoever corrects her.

<summary>The Friend advises the Lover to use extreme flattery, even lying about a woman's beauty, while warning that women naturally resist any form of correction or moral guidance.</summary>

Hunger, who sees neither wheat nor tree,

With sharp nails and hard teeth,
<margin>The description of hunger and famine.</margin>
But finds them very sparsely sprouted,
Sown among the thick rocks.
If I wished to describe her,
I might soon be delivered of the task.
¶ She is long and thin, weary and hollow;
Great is her need for bread of oats. <note>original: "pain dauoyne" — oat bread was considered a poor man's food, far inferior to the white wheat bread of the wealthy.</note>
Her hair is all standing on end,
Her eyes are deep-set and frozen,
Her face is pale and her lips are parched,
Her cheeks are rusted and stained. <note>original: "royllees" — likely referring to the crusty or discolored appearance of skin ravaged by malnutrition.</note>
One could see her entrails
Through the hard skin, if one wished.
The bones at her hips fail her,
Where all humors are lacking; <note>In medieval medicine, the "humors" were the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) thought to maintain health and vitality. Their absence here signifies a body near death.</note>
And she seems to have no belly at all,
Except for a place that sinks in so deep
That the whole chest of the girl
Rests against the ridge of her spine.
Thinness has lengthened her fingers,
The roundness of her knees is lost,
Her heels are high and protrude below;
It does not appear that she has any flesh within.

<summary>The text provides a gruesome personification of Hunger (Fain), described as a skeletal woman living in a barren, frozen wasteland at the edge of the world. This serves as a warning of the physical devastation caused by poverty and "foolish giving."</summary>

# THE ROMANCE

You have kept a fool by your side,
For no man can live without a fool
As long as he wishes to follow love,
For that is a crooked path
Where all good sense is overturned:
Good turns to evil, laughter to tears,
And joy to sadness and pain.
Yet he believes himself very wise
As long as he lives in such madness,
Which one ought not to call a life,
Such madness and frenzy;
For it is death and blindness,
And a labor without rest;
For through heat, one feels cold there,
And through cold, too great a heat.
Neither in winter nor in summer
Is there any stability in him
Who wishes to lead such a life;
For it brings poverty
To those who wish to follow love,<note>original: "suivre" (OCR transcription "fuire" is likely a misreading of the long 's'). The poem suggests that following Love leads to ruin, whereas fleeing it would lead to safety.</note>
Which does nothing but harm them.

Now know that when you believed her,
You were most falsely deceived,<note>This likely refers to the Lover's internal conflict; though he heard Reason, his heart deceived him into staying on the path of Love.</note>

Repents of it—that is a well-known thing—
And pays for it dearly
Before he reaches his end.
But before Reason arrived there...

# THE ROMANCE

He will repent of the transgression
And will not wish to deceive then;
He shall hold the romance so dear
That he will wish to finish it all,
If time and opportunity come to him.
For when Guillaume shall cease,
Jean shall continue it,
After his death—and I do not lie—
More than forty years having passed. <note>Jean de Meun (the second author) took up the poem approximately forty years after Guillaume de Lorris (the first author) died, leaving the work unfinished around line 4,050.</note>
And he shall say then, because of misfortune
And for fear of despair,
That he might not have lost from <term>Fair Welcome</term> <note>original: "Bel Accueil" — a personified character in the poem representing the Lady’s receptivity and kindness toward the Lover.</note>
The goodwill previously held.
"And so I have lost hope;
I am nearly in despair,"
And all the other words,
Whether they be wise or foolish,
Until he shall have plucked,
Upon the green leafy branch,
The most beautiful vermillion rose,
Before it is day and he awakes. <note>This is a prophetic summary of the poem's eventual ending, where the Lover finally gains the Rose and the dreamer wakes up.</note>
Then he will want to hide the matter so much
That no one will be able to offer a reply;
And if I could provide good counsel there,
I ought to advise promptly.
But by Guillaume it cannot be,
Nor by Jean, who is yet to be born,
For he is not present here;
Yet the case is so very pressing
That certainly, when he shall be born...

Before the time he is weaned,
From his double casks that he has, <note>This is a reference to the two jars of Homeric myth (attributed here to Jupiter/Zeus), one containing blessings and the other containing evils, which determine a person's fate.</note>

Because he is one of my friends,
I will cover him with my wings,
And will sing him such notes,
That once he is out of childhood,
Instructed in my knowledge—

### THE ROMANCE

He will pipe our words
Through crossroads and through schools,
According to the language of France <note>original: "langaige de france" — Jean de Meun was famous for writing in the vernacular (French) rather than Latin, making the work accessible to the general public as well as scholars.</note>
Throughout the kingdom in public hearing,
So that all those who hear them
Will not die of the "ills of loving," <note>original: "maux daymer" — a reference to the physical and emotional distress caused by unrequited or intense passion, a central theme in courtly love.</note>
Provided that they only believe him;
For he will write so skillfully
That all those who are yet to live
Should call this book
**The Mirror for Lovers,**
So much good will they see in it for themselves—
Provided that Reason is not believed,
That wretched, ill-mannered one. <note>original: "la chetiue la malostrue" — In the poem, the character Reason tries to persuade the Lover to abandon his pursuit. The God of Love here insults her as an enemy to his cause.</note>
For this I wish to take counsel here;
Each of you must give me counsel.
From among you, I pray and cry out to you,
That Guillaume, whom I so highly praise, <note>Guillaume de Lorris, the original author of the first 4,058 lines of the poem.</note>
Who has conducted himself so well toward me,
Be succored and comforted.
And even if I did not pray for him,
<margin>The God of Love’s conclusion.</margin> I certainly ought to pray,
At least now to lighten the burden for Jean,
So that he might write more easily,
That you grant him this advantage;
For he shall be born, I am his prophet.
And for the others who shall come,
Who will devoutly intend
To follow my commandments,
Which they will find written in the book.

I do not have my way with her in everything.
Yet she knows well how to come running
When she wishes to help me
And bring my affairs to an end.
But I do not wish to burden her;
She is my mother, and I have feared her since childhood."

### OF THE ROSE

By this, he cannot lose everything,
Even if he had to stick to the hide <note>The poet argues that if a man buys a physical horse, even in the worst case, he still owns the leather/hide of the animal.</note>,

Who knowingly buy a thing
And lose everything they put into it;
And it cannot remain their own,
No matter how hard they "labor" at it <note>original: "labourer" — this often carries a sexual double entendre in the *Rose*, referring to the physical act as well as the effort of the lover.</note>.
Notwithstanding, I do not seek to deny:
My mother knows nothing of paying.

<summary>The God of Love concludes his critique of transactional love, arguing that unlike a horse, a woman's affection cannot be truly bought because the "buyer" gains no exclusive rights or lasting value. He emphasizes that "foolish love" (prostitution or mercenary desire) is a poor investment where the merchant loses both his capital and his lordship.</summary>

Just as the cats do,

Is on a very dangerous path; 
It rarely happens that he is not either a thief 
Or a perjurer, or else the Scripture is greatly mistaken. 
For Solomon speaks aptly 
Regarding that which I propose to you.

And then I can well swear without deceit 
That it is not written in any law— 
At least it is not in ours— 
That Jesus Christ or His Apostles, 
As long as they walked upon the earth, 
Ever went about begging for their bread; 
For they did not wish to beg, 
Even though they were accustomed to preaching. 
Formerly in the city of Paris, 
The masters of divinity <note>This refers to the secular teachers at the University of Paris who, in the 13th century, were embroiled in a bitter conflict with the Mendicant Friars (Dominicans and Franciscans) over the right to teach and the morality of begging.</note>— 
Who could certainly ask for support 
By their full authority without being beggars— 
Were pastors on God’s behalf 
And had the care of souls. 
Even after the death of their Master, 
They began at once to be 
Industrious with their hands; 
From their labor, neither more nor less, 
They always received their sustenance.

<summary>False Seeming argues against the practice of religious begging (mendicancy), claiming that neither Christ nor the Apostles begged for bread, but instead supported themselves through manual labor.</summary>

# THE ROMANCE OF THE ROSE

<margin>Of the **usurers** <term>usurers</term> <note>original: *vsu-riers*; those who lend money at interest. In the medieval period, usury was considered a sin by the Church, yet it was a central part of the burgeoning urban economy.</note>.</margin>

# THE ROMANCE

<margin>False Seeming meddles in everything.</margin>
But however much we complain,
We are—let this be known to you—
Those who have everything while having nothing. <note>This paradox refers to the mendicant (begging) orders of the 13th century, who took vows of poverty yet accumulated significant power and resources.</note>
I meddle in brokerage <term>brokerage</term> <note>original: *courretaiges*; the act of being a middleman or agent. In this context, it implies meddling in private deals, legal matters, or even pimping.</note>

Which do not make me very honest;
To handle the business of others,
That is a most pleasant trade for me.
And if you have anything to do
Regarding those with whom I associate,
Tell it to me and the thing is done
As soon as you have voiced your intent. <note>original: *si tost que lame aurez retraicte*; literally "as soon as you have withdrawn the soul," meaning as soon as the thought has left your mind or been spoken.</note>
Because you have served me well,
You have deserved my service.

<margin>False Seeming hardly loves hermits.</margin>
But whoever would wish to chastise me
Would soon lose my favor.
I do not love nor value the man
By whom I receive any rebuke.
I wish to rebuke all others,
But I do not wish to hear their leader, <note>original: *prince*; likely referring here to the authority or the logic of those who would criticize him.</note>
For I, who chastises the others,
Have no need of outside correction.

I have no care for hermitages;
I leave the deserts and groves,

The manor and lodging of the desert,
For we would be cast too far away
From the towns, the castles, and cities.

# LE ROMMANT

It is written thus in the book
Which tells and signifies this:
As long as Peter holds the lordship,
John cannot show his strength.
I have told you the "bark" of the meaning, <note>original: *scorce*; literally "bark" or "rind." This is a common medieval metaphor for the literal or superficial meaning of a text, beneath which the "pith" or true intent is hidden.</note>

By "Peter," I mean the Pope,
And include the secular clergy, <term>secular clergy: priests and clerics who live "in the world" (the *seculum*) and serve in parishes or universities, as opposed to "regular" clergy who live under a monastic rule.</term>

By the "strength of John," understand
The grace of which he boasts,
Which seeks to convert the preachers <note>The text suggests the grace aims to turn these preachers toward God, or perhaps highlights their claim to be the only truly spiritual ones.</note>

<margin>The sophistries of old procuresses used to seduce women.</margin> <note>original: *Les cauillatiõs des vieilles macq̃reles*; "sophistries" or "quibbles" refers to the manipulative and deceptive arguments used by experienced go-betweens to lead young people into romance.</note>

But I conducted myself too foolishly;
I was beautiful, young, silly, and wild.
I never attended the school of Love
Where I might have read the **theory**,
But I know it all through **practice**.
<margin>Experience is the mistress of all things. Note. <note>original: *Experience maistresse de toutes choses. Nota.*</note></margin>
Experience has made me wise,
For I have frequented all circles in my time.

Without fail, it is no wonder
If you know not a bit of it,
For you have a **beak that is too yellow**, <note>original: *le bec trop iaulne*; a medieval idiom for being young and inexperienced, like a fledgling bird that still has the yellow coloring on its beak.</note>

Not obtained without great loss—
I have deceived many a valiant man

But before that, I was deceived by many.

Had I realized it then,

# LE ROMMANT

What pain was in my heart
From the memory and the heartbreak
<margin>Beauty is soon passed.</margin>
Of those beautiful gifts, pleasant and light,
Of sweet desires, of sweet kisses,
And of those pleasant embraces
Which were so quickly gone,
Gone, indeed, without return.
It would have been better for me
To be forever imprisoned in a tower
Than to have been born so soon.
Tell me what worry they put me in—
Those beautiful gifts that failed me—
And how the memory of what was left of them
Put me back into such torment.
Alas, why was I born so soon?
To whom should I complain, to whom,
Except to you, son, whom I hold so dear.
I cannot well rid myself of this pain
Except by showing you my <term>doctrine</term> <note>original: *doctrine*; here referring to her specialized "curriculum" or system of rules for navigating the games of love and seduction.</note>,
Therefore, fair son, I instruct you,
And when you are fully taught,
You shall avenge me upon those <term>scoundrels</term> <note>original: *ribaudeaulx*; meaning debauched men, rogues, or profligates who mistreat women.</note>,
For, if it pleases God, when the time comes,
You will remember this <term>sermon</term> <note>original: *sermon*; the Old Woman frames her advice as a formal moral discourse or lecture.</note>.
And know that of the memory—
So that you may truly remember it—
You will have a very great advantage
By reason of your <term>young age</term> <note>original: *bas aage*; literally "low age," meaning youth or early adolescence.</note>.
<margin>The teaching of Plato <note>original: *La setẽce de platõ*; referring to a maxim by the Greek philosopher.</note>.</margin>
For Plato says—and it is a true thing—
That the memory is more retentive...

<summary>The Old Woman expresses her deep grief over her lost youth and beauty, deciding to mentor Fair Welcome in her "doctrine" of love so he can avenge her against the men who abandoned her. ### OF THE ROSE

Of that which one learns in childhood,
It matters not to me from where the knowledge comes.
Certainly, dear son, in your tender <term>youth</term> <note>original: *iouuente*; referring to the prime of life, characterized by vigor and beauty.</note>,
If my youth were present,
Just as yours is right now,
No writing could adequately describe
The vengeance that I would then have taken;
For I held them all in great shame,
And I would then have performed such marvels
That you never heard the likes of them,
Against the <term>scoundrels</term> <note>original: *ribaulx*; a derogatory term for debauched or worthless men.</note> who value me so little,
And who insult and despise me,
And pass by me so vilely;
Those men and others would have paid for
Their great pride and their spite,
Without having pity or respite.
For with the wisdom that God has given me,
As I have preached to you,
Do you know into what state I would have put them?
I would have <term>plucked</term> them <note>original: *plumasse*; a frequent metaphor in this poem for stripping a lover of his money and possessions, much like plucking a bird's feathers.</note> so thoroughly and taken so much
Of their wealth, by hook or by crook,
That I would have left them for the worms to devour,
Lying all naked on dung-heaps—
Even those very men
Who loved me with the most loyal hearts,
And most loyally exerted themselves
To serve and honor me.
I would not have let them keep
The value of an onion, if I could help it,
Before I had it all in my purse.

# THE ROMANCE

<margin>The avarice of old **bawds** <note>original: *macquerelles*; a derogatory term for procuresses or aging women who live off the sex trade.</note>.</margin>
To great poverty I would have put them all,
And made them all, following after me,
Dance in a vivid frenzy;
But it is of no use to regret it,
For what is gone cannot return.
Never again will I be able to hold any man,
For my face is so wrinkled
That they have no fear of my threats.
Long ago, indeed, they told me so—
The **scoundrels** <note>original: *ribaulx*; refers to debauched men or those of low character.</note> who despised me,
Which is why I have now learned to weep.
By God, it still pleases me nonetheless
When I have well reflected on it,
And I greatly rejoice in my thoughts,
And my limbs are emboldened
When I remember my good times,

<margin>The old bawds regret the pleasure of time past.</margin>

It rejuvenates my whole body
When I think of it and recall it well;
It does me all the good in the world
When I remember the whole affair.
At least I had my joy then,
However much they may have greatly deceived me.

A young lady is not idle
When she leads a joyful life,
And especially she who thinks
To acquire enough to pay her expenses.

Then I came into this country
Where I encountered your lady.

## OF THE ROSE

¶ How the Old Woman, without quarreling,
Reads her lesson to Fair Welcome,
Which speaks quite clearly of women
Who are worthy of all **reproach** <note>original: *diffames*; meaning infamy or ill-repute. The rubricator suggests the Old Woman's advice reflects poorly on the character of women.</note>.

Fair son, you who wish to enjoy love,
And avoid every bitter ill,
Learn the **commandments of Love** <note>These refer to the formal rules of courtly conduct given by the God of Love to the Lover in the first half of the poem.</note>;
But take care that Love does not catch you in his snare.
And indeed, I would tell them all to you
Certainly, if I saw now
That you possessed them by nature,
In full and overflowing measure,
As many as you ought to have.
If you wish to know these "words,"
There are ten of them, for one who counts well;
But he is a great fool who burdens himself
<margin>The ten words of love.</margin>
With the final two,
Which are not worth a **false penny** <note>original: *faulx denier*; a counterfeit coin, implying the rules are worthless or even harmful.</note>.
I gladly grant you the other eight,
But whoever follows those last two
Wastes his study and loses his mind;
They should not be taught in any school.
It burdens lovers far too heavily
To require that a lover have a **generous heart** <term>Generous heart: originally *cueur large*, implying both emotional openness and, crucially, financial liberality or "largesse."</term>
And that he must devote himself to one single place;
That is false; it is a **false doctrine** <note>original: *faulce lettre*; literally "false letter," meaning a corrupted text or misleading teaching.</note>.
Though Love, the son of Venus, may desire it,
No one should believe him in this;
Whoever believes him will pay dearly for it.

## THE ROMANCE

And thus it will appear in the end.

<margin>The conditions that the lover must have.</margin>
My fair son, do not be **stingy** <note>original: *auers* (avaricious). While the God of Love commands the avoidance of stinginess to encourage generosity, the Old Woman repurposes the word to mean one should not withhold the *appearance* of love if it leads to profit.</note>;

Do not place it in one single spot,
Do not give it away, nor lend it,
But sell it quite dearly
And always by **driving up the price** <term>Driving up the price: originally *enchierement*, referring to the practice of increasing the perceived value or cost of one's favors through competition.</term>.
And take care that no one who buys it
Can make a good bargain of it;
Above all things, remember these points:
Keep your fists closed to giving,
And your hands open to taking.
For giving is certainly folly,
Except for a little bit to attract people
When one thinks it will serve their own interest,
Or to expect such a thing in return for the gift
That it could not be sold for less.
I allow you that kind of giving;
It is good to give, for he who gives
Multiplies his gift and profits
When he is certain of his **gain** <note>original: *gaigne*; the Old Woman views love as a commercial transaction where "giving" is merely an investment for a larger return.</note>.
One cannot repent of this;
I am happy to consent to such giving.

You shall shoot so wisely

<margin>One must not believe a scoundrel who commits perjury.</margin>
Jupiter and the gods used to laugh
When lovers committed perjury <note>original: *pariuroient*. To commit perjury or swear a false oath, especially in matters of love.</note>,
And many times they themselves swore falsely,
Those gods who loved for the sake of love;
For when Jupiter reassured
Juno his wife, and swore to her
Solemnly by the waters of hell <note>In Greek and Roman mythology, an oath taken by the River Styx—the "waters of hell"—was the most binding oath a god could take; to break it was to face divine punishment.</note>,

Should they not indeed grant license
<margin>The poets and gods swore by the depths of hell.</margin>
To fine lovers to swear falsely?
[By] saints and holy women, monasteries and temples,
Since the gods themselves set such examples.
But surely he is a great fool
Who believes any lover just because they swear,
Seeing that their hearts are far too changeable.
<margin>The perjury of lovers.</margin>
Young people are not stable,
And the old are often the same,
Breaking their word in their turn.
And know one thing to be true:
That the master and chief of the fair
Must collect his toll <note>original: *toulin*. A "tonlieu" was a tax or toll paid at a market or fair for the right to sell goods.</note> from everywhere;
And he who cannot go to one mill,
Let him take his path to another.
A mouse has poor resource,
And puts her life in great peril,
If she has only one hole for refuge.
Just so it is with the woman,
<margin>Comparison to a mouse.</margin>
Who is the mistress of all her markets;
She who does everything to have [suitors]
Should take wealth from everyone.

In the book of the heart, willingly,
All my commandments in their entirety,
When you now depart from me,
If it pleases God, you will read them again,

Less coveted, and less sought after.

<page-num>XXXVI</page-num>
<header>THE ROMANCE</header>

<margin>The authority of Sallust.</margin>
Because of the nature of truth,
And for this reason I have written thus,
For it is a very right and just thing,
By the authority of Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–34 BCE), a Roman historian. Jean de Meun is referencing Sallust’s idea from the *Bellum Catilinae* that the historian’s task is difficult because the words must match the deeds described.</note>
Who tells us through a true maxim
That there is not an equal glory
For the one who performs a deed
And for the writer who performs his task—
Who wishes to put it properly into a book
To better describe the truth.
For it is not a light matter,
But rather a very great undertaking
To put deeds properly into writing;
For whoever writes of a matter,
If he does not wish to stray from the truth,
The word must resemble the deed;
For words that are neighbors to things
Must be cousins to their deeds <note>original: "les voix... doiuent estre a leurs faictz cousines." This famous medieval literary principle is ultimately derived from Plato’s *Timaeus*. It argues that if a writer describes something "foul" or "plain," they must use "foul" or "plain" language to be truthful.</note>.
So it is necessary for me to speak this way,
Since I wish to follow the path of what is right.

### Excuses himself to the ladies of the Romance.

I pray you all, valiant women,
Whether you are young maidens or noble ladies,
Whether in love or without lovers,
That if you find words already set down
Which seem biting along the way
Against feminine manners <note>original: "meurs feminins"; this refers to the character, habits, or social conduct of women. Jean de Meun is preparing to excuse the misogynistic critiques voiced by certain characters in the poem.</note>

</margin>

Which are in accord with my reasoning

They were neither fools nor drunkards
When they put them into their books.
They knew feminine manners,
For they had experienced them all.

### OF THE ROSE

However great a sinner I may be,
I sent my arrow <note>original: "saiette"</note> flying
In general to strike them down—
Not to strike them down, but to expose
Those, whether of the world <note>Those living outside of monastic orders.</note> or of the cloister,
<margin>Note on the hypocrites</margin>
The cursed, disloyal people
Whom Jesus calls hypocrites,
Of whom many, to appear more honorable,
Refrain from eating the flesh of beasts
At all times in the name of penance,
And thus perform their abstinence
Just as when we are in **Lent** <note>original: "karesme"; the 40-day period of fasting before Easter.</note>;
But they eat men alive
With the teeth of detraction <note>The act of belittling someone's reputation; slander.</note>
And poisonous intent.
I never made my voice a herald of any other blood,
And I wish for my blade to miss its mark.
I shot at them at random <note>original: "a la volee"; meaning he aimed at a group or a vice generally, rather than a specific person.</note>,
And if, to receive a blow,
It happens that beneath the arrow
Some man places himself of his own will,
Who deceives himself through pride
So that he receives the blow upon himself,
<margin>Note.</margin>
Then complains that I have wounded <note>original: "naure"</note> him,
I have no guilt for it, nor will I ever have,
Not even if he were to perish from it;
For I cannot strike anyone
Who wishes to guard himself from the blow,
If he knows how to examine his own state.
Even he who feels himself wounded

### THE ROMANCE
### XC VIII

By the iron <note>Referring to the tip of the arrow mentioned on the previous page.</note> that is now before him,
Let him take care no longer to be a hypocrite,
And he shall be healed of his wound.
And yet, no matter who complains of it,

And if there is any word

I am ready to amend it at her will,

¶ Here the author resumes his tale without fail,
And comes to the battle
Where Lady **Franchise** <note>The personification of Generosity, Frankness, or Nobility of Spirit.</note> fights

In his fist he holds a **club** <note>original: "massue"</note>,
Fiercely he brandishes and swings it
Around himself with perilous blows,
So that no shield, however marvelous,
Could resist without him shattering it.

[Those] who do not fear death at all
And yet they go on decaying
And die in their time and rot,
Upon which other things feed <note>A reference to the biological cycle where the decay of one organism provides nutrients for others, a concept Jean de Meun uses to show the continuity of life despite individual death.</note>.
When [Death] thinks to catch them all,

Another on that side escapes him.
For when he has killed the father,
There remains the son, daughter, or mother,
Who flee before death

Then it becomes necessary for these to die too,
No matter how well they know how to run;
Medicine is of no value or help <note>original: "Medicine ny vault ne veulx"; expressing the medieval sentiment that while medicine exists, it cannot ultimately conquer mortality.</note>,
Whereby nieces and nephews fail,
Who flee to carry themselves away
As far as their feet can carry them.
Wherefore one flees, another dances <note>original: "carolle"; the carole was a popular medieval circle dance accompanied by singing, here representing those who distract themselves from death through social merriment.</note>,

And others to their pleasures

Others, to flee even faster

# THE ROMANCE

Of alchemy <term>Darquemie: An archaic form of "alchemy." In this context, Jean de Meun refers to it as a "true art" because it works with the actual elements of nature rather than just mimicking outward appearances.</term> and the true art,
Whoever would work wisely at it
Would find great wonders there;
For however it may be with the species,
At least individual parts,
Subjected to physical operations,
Are changeable in so many ways
That their physical constitutions,
Through various "digestions" <term>Digeſtions: In medieval alchemy, this refers to the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat over a long period, mimicking the digestive process to refine, ripen, or transform matter.</term>,
Can change so much among themselves that these changes
Place them under strange species
And strip away their original species.
<margin>The subtle skill of making glass from fern.</margin> Does one not see how from the fern,
Once turned to ash, one sees glass produced? <note>original: "voirre mettre". The poet refers to the medieval practice of creating "forest glass" (potash glass). Ferns were burned to create potash, which was then melted with sand to create glass—a process that seemed like a miraculous transmutation of a plant into a stone-like substance.</note>
He who is a skilled master knows this well,
Through a simple purification;
Yet the glass is not the fern,
Nor is the fern the glass.
And when lightning or thunder comes,
Can one not very often see
<margin>Stones in the air engendered from vapors.</margin> Stones fall from great vapors,
Which did not ascend as stones. <note>This refers to the medieval meteorological theory that "thunderstones" (meteorites) were formed when dry, earthy vapors rose into the clouds and were compressed and baked into stone by the heat of lightning.</note>
He can understand this who knows the path
Of the cause that draws such matter
Into this strange species.
Thus are the species changed,
And their parts transformed from their former selves,
Both in substance and in form—
Some by Art, others by Nature.

And because, if I could have succeeded <note>original: "cheuisse". From the Old French *chevir*, meaning to achieve, master, or come to an end of a task.</note>,

# ON THE ROMANCE CCCVIII

He does not stir for a small thing;
He is a fool who dares to trouble you.
But without fail, it is true that a woman
Easily becomes inflamed in her speech,
<margin>The judgment of Virgil on the fickleness of women.</margin>
Virgil himself testifies to it,
Who knew much of their behavior,
That a woman is never so stable
That she is not diverse and fickle <note>original: "muable". This refers to the medieval trope of *mutabilitas*, the idea that women were naturally prone to change and inconsistency.</note>
And is a much worse, hideous beast.
<margin>Solomon</margin>
Solomon says that there was never a head
On a cruel serpent-beast
That was more wrathful than a woman;
And no thing has such great malice,
For in woman lies so much vice
That no one can count her perverse ways
In rhyme or in verse.
<margin>Titus Livius <note>The Roman historian Livy.</note></margin>
And so says Titus Livius,
Who well knew what their habits are,
And also their manners:
That toward their ways, no prayers
Are worth as much as flatteries <term>blandishments: flattering speech or actions used to persuade or coax.</term>
They are so deceptive and foolish <note>original: "nices". In Middle French, this means simple, ignorant, or foolish, rather than "pleasant."</note>
And of a flexible nature.
Furthermore, Scripture says elsewhere
That of all feminine vice,
The foundation is avarice,
<margin>A note on not telling one's secret to one's wife.</margin>
And whoever tells his wife
His secrets, he makes her his master.
No one who was ever born of a mother [would do so],
Unless he were very drunk or mad.

<summary>Genius provides a misogynistic justification for Nature's distress by citing authorities like Virgil, Solomon, and Livy to claim that women are inherently fickle, wrathful, and untrustworthy with secrets. This passage reflects the medieval tradition of "the mal de femme," or the catalog of perceived feminine vices common in academic and courtly debates.</summary>

# THE ROMANCE OF THE ROSE

The planets do a great and noble work, for each of them labors so much that none of the seven ever rests. They turn through their twelve houses <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac, which were viewed as "houses" or stations for the planets.</note> and run through every degree, remaining there as long as they must. And to perform their task well, they turn with a contrary motion <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the planets were believed to move from West to East, contrary to the "daily" rotation of the outer heavens which moved from East to West.</note>. Each day they gain upon the heavens the portions that belong to them in order to complete their orbital circles; then they begin again without ceasing, following the course of the heavens to bring aid to the elements <note>The four elements—Earth, Water, Air, and Fire—which make up the world below the moon and are influenced by celestial movements.</note>. For if the sky could run merely for its own pleasure, nothing could survive beneath it.

<margin>The description of the sun.</margin>
The beautiful sun, which brings the day and is the source of all brightness, takes its place in the center like a king, all radiant with its beams. It sits in its house in the midst of the others, and this is by no means without reason; for God—the Beautiful, the Strong, the Wise—willed that its station be there. For if it ran more slowly, there is nothing that would not perish from the heat, and if it ran at a higher altitude, the cold would bring everything to ruin <note>Medieval science held that the Sun was positioned in the middle of the seven planetary spheres (with three above it and three below) to perfectly balance the temperature of the Earth.</note>. From there, it distributes its shared light...

# THE ROMANCE

<margin>The sun illuminates the other planets.</margin>
The sun gives light to the stars and to the moon and makes them appear so beautiful that Night makes them her candles in the evening when she sets her table, so as to be less terrifying before Acheron, my husband <note>In this section of the poem, Nature is the narrator. She refers to Acheron, traditionally a river of the underworld, as her husband, though medieval poets often played with these mythological genealogies to illustrate the interconnectedness of natural forces.</note>, who has a very heavy heart because of it; for he would much rather be without any light and remain with Night in total darkness, just as they were together when they first knew one another.

<margin>Night, mother of the Furies of hell, according to the poets.</margin>
It was when Night was in their frenzy that she conceived the three rages <note>The Furies (Tisiphone, Megaera, and Alecto), the vengeful deities who punished crimes; in classical mythology, they were often said to be the daughters of Night.</note> who are the dispensers of justice in hell—cruel, wicked, and proud. But nevertheless, Night now considers, as she looks at herself in her pantry, in her cellar, or in her cave, that she would be most hideous and haggard, and her face would be far too gloomy, if she did not have the joyous clarity of the resplendent celestial bodies shining through the darkened air, which turn within their sphere as God the Father established them.

<margin>The harmony of the heavens.</margin>

# OF THE ROSE CCCXIX

Through her <note>Nature is speaking of her own power and the cosmic order she maintains.</note>, everything changes and varies, and through their influences, **accidents** <term>Accidents: In medieval philosophy, these are the non-essential properties of a thing (like color or temperature) as opposed to its core essence.</term> and **substances** are transformed. <margin>The four different qualities.</margin>

She goes about binding them together and makes peace between four enemies <note>The "four enemies" are the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) or the four elements (fire, air, water, earth), which were thought to be in constant opposition.</note> once she has put them together through a suitable **tempering** <term>Tempering (attrempance): The act of balancing opposing qualities to achieve a stable state.</term> into a reasonable **complexion** <term>Complexion: A person’s unique physical and mental constitution, determined by the balance of the four humors or qualities.</term> to form, in the best possible shape, all the things that I <note>Nature</note> form. If death comes otherwise, as if hastened by other circumstances—

That divine prescience <note>original: "prescience divine"—God's capacity to know all things before they happen.</note>

# OF THE ROSE

If they are too melancholic <note>original: "melencolieux" — in medieval medicine, an excess of "black bile" (melancholy) was believed to cause hallucinations, dark visions, and unfounded fears.</note> or too fearful beyond measure, they cause many diverse figures to appear within themselves, differently than what we described seeing when we spoke of mirrors—which we passed over so briefly—and it seems to them then that all these things are truly there on the outside.

<margin>Note on the Dream of Scipio</margin> <note>This refers to the *Somnium Scipionis*, a famous passage from Cicero's "Republic" that was widely read in the Middle Ages as a guide to the afterlife and the cosmos.</note>

For they have too many other things to attend to.
Therefore, as they may well know,
Scholars have more and greater advantages
<margin>Note.</margin>
Than do earthly lords
For attaining **nobility**
And for conquering gentility...

<summary>Nature argues that scholars (clerics) have a greater duty to be virtuous because their education gives them direct access to moral teachings. She asserts that an educated person who chooses vice is more contemptible than an uneducated person or a king distracted by worldly affairs.</summary>

### OF THE ROSE

<margin>Note the rules of the noble-born.</margin>
To whoever is most honorable on earth,
All those who wish to possess it <note>Referring to "gentilleſſe" or true nobility of spirit mentioned on the previous page.</note>
Must know this rule.
Whoever has any **nobility** <note>original: "gentilleſſe" — In this context, it refers to the inherent quality of being "gentle" or noble in character, which Nature argues is a practiced virtue.</note>

Let them go to arms <note>Engage in military service or knightly training.</note> or to study,
And rid themselves of **villainy** <note>original: "villenie" — This refers to the crude, base, or immoral behavior associated with those who lack courtly education.</note>.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Honor ladies and young maidens,

Knights bold in arms
Are valiant in deeds and "cowardly" in speech <note>original: "couars en dis" — This is a courtly ideal: a knight should be fierce in battle but modest and humble when speaking of his own exploits.</note>,

Who was never afraid without cause.
<margin>The virtuous Count of Artois</margin>

Who, from the moment he left the cradle,
Practiced every day of his life
Generosity, honor, and **chivalry**.
Idle rest never pleased him;
Instead, he became a man before his time.
Such a knight, brave and valiant...

<summary>Nature outlines the code of conduct for true nobility, emphasizing that it requires a rejection of pride and idleness in favor of military service, study, and humility. She cites Sir Gawain and Robert of Artois as historical and literary models of these chivalric virtues.</summary>

# THE ROMANCE

Generous and bold, a good fighter
Should be welcomed everywhere,
Praised, loved, and held dear.
One should greatly honor the **scholar** <note>original: "clerc" — In the medieval period, a "cleric" or scholar was defined by his literacy and education rather than just his religious status. Nature argues that their intellectual work is a form of noble labor.</note>
Who wishes to work with good sense,
And thinks to follow the virtues
That he sees written in his book.
And certainly, this was done in the past;
I could easily name ten of them,
Indeed, so many that if I counted them,
It would be tiresome to hear the number.
In the past, every valiant nobleman—
As the people name them:
Emperors, dukes, counts, and kings,
Whom I shall no longer list here—

<margin>Philosophers and poets were formerly honored.</margin>

They honored the philosophers
And even gave to the poets
Cities, gardens, honorable places,
And many delightful things.
**Naples** was given to **Virgil** <note>In medieval legend, the Roman poet Virgil was often depicted as a powerful magician and a patron of Naples, where he was said to have performed many wonders.</note>,
Which is a more honorable city
Than Amiens, or even Lavardin.
In **Calabria** he had very beautiful gardens
At that time, which were given to him
By the ancients who knew him.
But why should I name more,
When I could prove it by many others
Who were born of low lineage
And yet had **nobler spirits** <note>original: "nobles couraiges" — Here "couraige" refers to the heart, spirit, or inner character rather than just bravery.</note>
Than ever the sons of kings and counts.

# OF THE ROSE

Of these I will not give you an account here,
Though they were held as noble.
But now the times have come to this:
That the good men who, all their lives,
Labor in **philosophy** <note>original: "philosophie" — In the Middle Ages, "philosophy" encompassed nearly all secular learning, including science, ethics, and logic.</note>
And travel into foreign lands
To gain wisdom and honor,
And who suffer great poverty
Like beggars and debtors,

They are neither loved nor held dear.
Princes do not value them at two apples,
And yet they are more valiant men
(May God save me from the "figs" <note>original: "ficures" — Likely a colloquial reference to "fics," which were painful growths or hemorrhoids. This is a bit of medieval humor: the narrator uses a common ailment of the sedentary scholar as an oath to emphasize their point.</note>)
Than those who go hunting for **hares**
Or those who are accustomed
To catching birds with **sparrowhawks** <note>original: "esperviers" — Hunting with birds of prey was the quintessential pastime of the landed nobility; Nature is contrasting the scholar’s "valiance" with the nobleman’s leisure.</note>.

<margin>Take note.</margin>

He who, from another’s nobility,
Without his own worth and **prowess**,
Wishes to carry off praise and renown—
Is he noble? I say he is **not**.
Instead, he should be called a **churl** <note>original: "vilain" — In medieval terminology, a "vilain" was a person of low social rank, but the term also carried a heavy moral weight, implying a lack of manners or virtue.</note>
And held as vile and less loved

I will not go about mocking anyone,
Even if he were the son of **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great, who was the ultimate historical model for world-conquering kingship in the medieval imagination.</note>,
Who dared to take up arms so much,
And continued his wars so long,
That he became the lord of all lands.

<summary>Nature laments the decline of respect for scholars, arguing that a poor philosopher is more truly "valiant" than a nobleman who spends his time hunting. She concludes that nobility is not inherited; even the son of Alexander the Great would be a "churl" if he lacked personal merit.</summary>

He can understand nothing else

<meta>This page continues Nature's discourse on the origins of true nobility. # OF THE ROSE CCCLI

If he wounds his parents’ reputation,
And if he does not wish to live
In such a way that he follows their deeds—
He who wishes to resemble a nobleman,
If he does not want to steal the title of **nobility** <note>original: "gentilleſſe" — In the Middle Ages, this term referred both to high birth and the moral excellence expected of a "gentleman." Nature argues here that birth without virtue is a form of theft.</note>
And have **praise** <note>original: "loz" — From the Latin 'laus', meaning reputation or renown.</note> without deserving it,
I make it known to him for truth
That nobility bestows nothing
Unless it is good,
<margin>Note.</margin>
Excluding deeds alone.
And know very certainly
That no one should receive praise
By the virtue of another person.
Likewise, it is not right that I blame
Any person for the faults of another.
Let him be praised who deserves it;
But he who performs no good,
In whom one finds wickedness,
**Vulgarity** <note>original: "villenies" — Referring to the traits of the 'villain' or churl, the conceptual opposite of the 'gentil' or noble.</note> and enmity,
And boastings and **ostentation** <note>original: "boubans" — Extravagant display or excessive pride in one's status.</note>,
Or he who is deceitful and **flattering** <note>original: "lobans" — Someone who deceives through trickery or false praise.</note>,
Stuffed with pride and **mockery** <note>original: "rampoſnes" — Contemptuous or insulting language.</note>,
Without charity and without alms,
And negligent and lazy—
For one finds quite a few of these,
Though they be born of parents
In whom all virtues were apparent—
It is not just to say, or to grant praise,
That he should have the renown of his parents;
Instead, he should be held more vile [for his failings]...

<summary>In this passage, Nature explains that true nobility is a product of one's own virtuous actions rather than the reputation of one's ancestors. She argues that those born to noble parents who lead lives of vice are more contemptible than the low-born because they have squandered their heritage.</summary>

# THE ROMANCE

Though he were the son of a base man.

<margin>Note.</margin>
<margin>
Wisdom and 
prowess 
are the 
opposites of 
avarice.
</margin>
Let every reasonable man know
That it is not at all the same thing
To acquire **wisdom** <note>original: "sens" — In this context, it refers to both common sense and the higher cultivation of the mind.</note> and **nobility** <note>original: "gentilleſſe" — Refers to the moral and social excellence of a true gentleman or lady.</note>
And renown through **prowess** <note>original: "proueſſe" — The valor or skill typical of a knight.</note>
As it is to acquire great **holdings** <note>original: "tenemens" — Feudal land tenures or properties held from a superior lord.</note>,
Great wealth and great **finery** <note>original: "aornemens" — Decorative luxuries, jewelry, or elaborate clothing that displayed status.</note>
To use according to their desires,
For those who are inclined
To toil in order to acquire much—
Great wealth, finery, or land—
Though they have treasures amassed,
A hundred thousand **marks** <note>original: "marcs" — A medieval unit of weight for gold or silver, representing a vast sum of money.</note> or even more,
They will leave it all to their friends,
But those who have put their labor
Into the other things mentioned above,
So that they possess them by their own merits,
**Love** <note>original: "Amours" — Likely referring to the person's own attachments or perhaps a personification of the force of desire; some versions of the text use "Atropos" (Death) here to signify that even death cannot strip a man of his virtue to give it to another.</note> cannot so constrain them

Can they leave behind **knowledge** <note>original: "ſcience" — In the medieval sense, this means formal learning or a branch of study.</note>? No.
Nor nobility, nor renown;
But they can teach them to their heirs
If the heirs wish to take an example from them.
They can do nothing else in the matter,
Nor can the heirs extract anything more from them;
If they do not recreate these virtues themselves, they have no power,
Nor would they be worth a scrap of bark,
But they think of nothing except having
Possessions and wealth.

<summary>Nature explains that while material wealth and land can be inherited by heirs, true nobility, wisdom, and renown are non-transferable qualities that each individual must earn through their own merit and effort.</summary>

And every man calls himself a **nobleman** <note>original: "gentil homme" — In the Middle Ages, this referred to a man of "gentle" birth, implying he belongs to the aristocracy.</note>
Because he is addressed as such,
And because his good parents were so

Those who boast of another’s nobility

In their deeds or in their manner of being.

Had not death made them strangers to it—
Death, which through mortal difference
Creates the separation of men.
And let them seek new nobilities

For if they do not acquire it through their own efforts,
They will never be noble through another’s [merit].

I exclude from this neither duke nor count;

# OF THE ROSE CCCLIII

Who can well explain the cause of these?
**Flying dragons** <note>original: "Dragons volans" — A medieval term for bolides or bright meteors that leave a trail, appearing like mythical creatures in the night sky.</note> and sparks
Make them seem like candles in the air
Which descend, falling from the heavens,
As **simple people** <note>The "simple gens" refers to those without formal education in natural philosophy who interpret physical events as supernatural signs.</note> understand it.
But Reason cannot well see
That anything could fall from the high heavens;
For in them there is nothing **corruptible** <note>Refers to the Aristotelian belief that the "celestial spheres" above the moon were perfect, unchanging, and indestructible, unlike the "sublunary" world of Earth where things decay.</note>,
So pure, fine, strong, and stable are they.
Neither do they receive any marks
Which are imprinted from the outside,
Nor could anything break them,
And they would let nothing pass through
However subtle or permeable it might be,
Unless it were a **spiritual thing**.
Their rays certainly pass through there,
But they do not damage or break anything.
The hot summers and the cold winters
They create through their various **aspects** <note>original: "regars" — In astrology and astronomy, the "regard" or aspect is the angular relationship between planets which was believed to influence Earthly weather and events.</note>,
And they produce the snows and the hailstones—
<margin>Many impressions in the sky.</margin>
One hour large, the next hour small—
And many other **impressions** <note>original: "impreſſions" — In medieval science, this term referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, rainbows, meteors, and comets.</note>
According to their compositions,
And according to how they move apart,
Or approach, or join together.
Because of this, many people are often dismayed
When they see **eclipses** in the sky,
And they believe themselves to be in peril
From the gazes fixed upon them
By the planets they have seen.

V i

<summary>Nature explains that celestial phenomena like meteors ("flying dragons") and eclipses are natural results of planetary movements and atmospheric conditions rather than supernatural omens. She asserts the Aristotelian view that the high heavens are incorruptible and distinct from the changing atmosphere of Earth.</summary>

Whereof they so quickly lose sight,
But if they knew the **causes** <note>original: "causes" — In medieval Aristotelian philosophy, understanding the "cause" of a phenomenon was the key to true knowledge (science) and the remedy for superstitious fear.</note> well,
They would never be troubled by anything,
Not even by the whistling of the winds
Or the rising waves of the sea
Making **billows** <note>original: "flocz" — archaic term for waves or floods.</note> that kiss the clouds,
Then afterwards the sea calming itself
So much that it dares no longer growl
Nor make its waves rebound,
Except for Him who by His knowledge
Makes the water move always
And makes it **ebb and flow**; <note>original: "aller & venir" — literally "go and come," a reference to the tides which medieval scholars attributed to the moon's influence or divine orchestration.</note>
Nothing exists that could restrain it.

And he who would like to inquire further
Of the wonders that occur on earth,
Of the course of the heavens and the stars,
He would find so many beautiful things
<margin>The stars of the sky are innumerable.</margin>
That he would never have written it all,
Whoever would want to put it all in writing.
Thus the sky fulfills its duty toward me,
Which by its goodness profits so much
That I can well perceive
That all perform their duty very well.
Nor do I complain of the **elements**; <note>The four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>
They keep my commands well,
They perform their **mixtures** <note>original: "mixtions" — The process by which the four primary elements combine to create all physical matter in the world.</note> well among themselves,
Turning in **revolutions**; <note>Refers to the cyclical nature of physical changes and the orbits of the celestial bodies.</note>
For whatever the moon has beneath it
Is **corruptible**, <note>original: "corruptible" — In the medieval worldview, the "sublunary" sphere (everything below the moon) was subject to change, decay, and death, unlike the eternal heavens above.</note> I know it well.

<summary>Nature explains that natural wonders like the tides and the weather are governed by divine and natural laws rather than being causes for fear. She asserts that the four elements and the sublunary world correctly follow her commands, though acknowledging that everything below the moon is subject to decay.</summary>

### CCCLIIII

->**OF THE ROSE**<-

<margin>Note on the completion of all natural things.</margin>
Nothing can be so well nourished
That it does not eventually **decay**; <note>original: "pourrir" — In the medieval view, all things composed of the four elements are subject to "generation and corruption," meaning they must eventually break down and die.</note>
All things have, by their **complexion**, <term>complexion</term> <note>A technical term in medieval physiology referring to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a creature's physical and mental nature.</note>
By natural intention,
A rule that neither fails nor lies;
Everything is under its command.
So general is this rule
That none fail or stray from it.

<margin>The trees obey Nature.</margin>
Likewise, I do not complain of the plants,
Which are not slow to obey;
They are very attentive to my laws,
And remain so as long as they are alive.
Their roots and their little leaves,
Trunks and branches, fruits and flowers,
Each and every one brings them forth
As much as it can until it is dead—
Like trees, herbs, and bushes.

<margin>Birds and fish are subject to Nature.</margin>
The birds also, and the fish,
Which are so beautiful to look upon,
Well do they know how to keep my rules;
All **breed** <note>original: "faonnent" — literally "to fawn," here used broadly for the reproduction of all animals.</note> according to their custom,
And bring honor to their lineage,
And do not let themselves fall away,
Which is a very great joy to behold.
I do not complain of the other beasts,
Whose heads I make incline
To look always toward the earth;
They never made war against me,
But all follow my **lead**. <note>original: "a ma cordelle tirent" — literally "pull at my cord," an idiom meaning they are under her direct control or follow her guidance like a leashed animal.</note>

¶ This powerful excommunication

No emasculated man, certainly,
Has any boldness within him,
Unless it be perhaps in some vice
To commit some great malice,
For in carrying out great devilries
All women are all too bold. <note>This reflects the frequent misogynistic interjections found in the later parts of the Romance of the Rose, where Jean de Meun equates female nature with a capacity for deceit and malice.</note>
Emasculated men resemble them in this,
Because their characters are similar.
In such a way, even if that emasculated man
Were not soiled by any other way of life
Or had committed no mortal sin,
At least he has sinned this much:
That he has done great wrong to Nature
By taking away his power of procreation <note>original: "engendrure"; the ability to generate life and continue the species.</note>,
For which no one could excuse him.

<summary>This page details the philosophical and character-based consequences of emasculation, arguing that it strips a man of his natural boldness and "humanity," rendering him "feminine" and cowardly. The text emphasizes that castration is a profound sin against Nature because it destroys the divine purpose of procreation.</summary>

Indeed, one could not think well of it—
At least I could not; for if I thought upon it
And recounted the truth of the matter,
I would sooner wear out my tongue
Than the defender <note>original: "scuseur"; referring to someone trying to justify Jupiter's actions.</note> could excuse him
For such a sin and such a crime,
So greatly has he wronged Nature. <note>In the poem, Nature is a personified character who represents the creative and procreative force of the universe. Jupiter’s act of castration is seen as a crime against the very ability to create life.</note>
But whatever sin it might be,
Jupiter took no account of it,
For he did this so that he might come to power
And hold the kingdom in his hand.
And when he had become king,
And was held as lord of the world,
He issued his commandments,
His laws and his decrees,
And soon had it all delivered
To teach the people how to live,
Crying out his proclamation in public,
Of which I will tell you the meaning.

->¶ How Jupiter had it preached<-
->That everyone take what they held most dear<-
->And do with it as they pleased,<-
->Entirely and according to their will.<-

Jupiter, who rules the world,
Commands and establishes by rule
That everyone should think of being at ease,
And if they know of something that pleases them,
They should do it, if they are able to do so...

# OF THE ROSE. CCCLXXIIII

To draw the crowds to his heart,
He never preached otherwise.
He generally granted
That everyone, by their own right, should do
Whatever they saw as pleasurable,
For pleasure, as he thought,
Is the best thing there is
And the sovereign good in life
Which everyone should desire.
And so that all would follow him
And take his deeds as a pattern,
He made an example of his way of living
By doing with his body whatever pleased him.

<margin>Jupiter, a man of pleasure.</margin>
Lord Jupiter the joyous,
By whom pleasure was so highly prized—
As he says in his *Georgics*,
He who also wrote the *Bucolics*, <note>Referring to the Roman poet Virgil (70–19 BC). Jean de Meun frequently cites classical authorities to lend weight to his narrative.</note>
As he found in the Greek books;
By his great wisdom, he proved much
Regarding how there was no one to drive the plow
Before he [Jupiter] came into his reign.
No one had ever plowed a field,
Nor hoed, nor tilled the soil,
And no boundaries had been set
By the simple, peaceful, and good people.
In common they sought among themselves
The goods that came of their own accord. <note>This describes the "Golden Age," a mythological period of peace and communal living that preceded the reign of Jupiter, during which humanity lived without labor or private property.</note>

<margin>Jupiter first divided the earth.</margin>
He commanded the earth to be divided,
Where previously no one knew how to claim a share,
And he partitioned it by acres, <note>original: "arpens"; an ancient French unit of land measurement roughly equivalent to an acre.</note>

<summary>This page describes Jupiter's transition from the communal Golden Age to a new era defined by the pursuit of personal pleasure and the invention of private property through the division of land.</summary>

# THE ROMANCE. CCCLXXV

<margin>The inventions of Jupiter.</margin>
He put venom into the snakes
And taught the wolves to prey; <note>In the Golden Age, animals were thought to be peaceful; Jupiter introduced predatory behavior.</note>
So much did he cause malice to climb on high.
He cut open the oaks in the middle <note>According to classical myth, honey used to drip spontaneously from oak trees; Jupiter stopped this flow, forcing humans to work for their food.</note>
And stayed the running streams of wine.
He caused the fire to be extinguished everywhere,
Waking himself so fully to subdue the people,
And made them seek fire within the stone, <note>A reference to the discovery of flint; fire was no longer a gift but something that required effort to produce.</note>
So subtle and full of craft was he.
He created various new arts,
And gave names and numbers to the stars.
He had snares, nets, and traps set
To capture wild beasts,
And gave them dogs for the first time,
To which no one before was accustomed.
He tamed the birds of prey
Through the malice that sharpens mankind.
He set assaults in places of battle
Between sparrowhawks, partridges, and quails,
And created tournaments in the clouds
Of goshawks, falcons, and cranes,
And made them come to the lure. <note>original: "loirre"; a tool used in falconry to call a hawk back to the hunter.</note>
And to maintain their favor,
So that they would return to the hand,
He often took them out evening and morning.
<margin>Note.</margin>
Thus the young lord <note>original: "damoiseaulx"; referring to Jupiter as a youthful, vigorous usurper of his father's throne.</note> did so much
That man is now a servant to many birds,
And has placed himself in their service—
They who before were enemies
And like horrible ravishers.

# THE ROMANCE OF THE ROSE. CCCLXXV

<margin>Note.</margin>
To the other peaceful little birds
Which he could not follow through the air,
Yet without their flesh he did not wish to live,
But rather desired to be their eater,
So much was he a delightful glutton <note>original: "lecheur"; literally a 'licker' or 'lecher,' here referring to a refined gluttony or gourmet appetite.</note>
And held the birds as dear delicacies.
He put the ferrets into the dens
And caused the rabbits <note>original: "connins"; the Middle French term for rabbits.</note> to be attacked
To make them fall into the nets.
That one [Jupiter] took such care for his own body
To scald, roast, and skin
The fish of the seas and the rivers;
And he created entirely new sauces
Of spices of various kinds,
In which he placed many herbs.

Thus did the arts <note>In this context, "arts" refers to human skills, technologies, and crafts developed out of necessity.</note> come forward,
For all things are conquered
By labor, by harsh poverty,
By which people are held in great care <note>original: "cure"; meaning worry, anxiety, or intense preoccupation.</note>,
For hardships stir their wits <note>original: "engins"; meaning both the mechanical 'engines' or traps and the 'ingenuity' of the human mind.</note>
Through the anguish that they find there,
As Ovid says, who had
Enough throughout the time he lived
Of good, of evil, of boredom, and shame,
As he himself recounts. <note>A reference to the Roman poet Ovid, whose works—particularly the *Metamorphoses*—frequently describe the transition between the ages of the world and his own personal exile.</note>
Truly Jupiter intended nothing,
When he strove to come to the earth,
Except to change the state of the empire
From good to bad, and from bad to worse.

<summary>This page describes how Jupiter’s reign introduced the arts of hunting small game and sophisticated cooking, concluding with the philosophical argument that human ingenuity and technology (the "arts") are born from the struggle against poverty and hardship.</summary>

# THE ROMANCE

<margin>
The year
divided into
four
parts.
</margin>
He <note>Referring to Jupiter, who overthrew his father Saturn to end the Golden Age.</note> was a very poor administrator of justice
And he caused the springtime to diminish
And divided the year into four parts
Just as they are divided at present:
Summer, autumn, spring, and winter—
These are the four different seasons.
Springtime used to hold sway over all, <note>In the Golden Age, it was believed to be perpetual spring.</note>
But Jupiter wished for this no longer,
He who turned his attention to ruling
And the Ages of Gold passed away.

<margin>
The worsening
of people
denoted by
the change
of metals.
</margin>
And now he made the Ages of Silver,
Which afterwards were of brass, for the people
Never ceased from then on to worsen,
So much did they wish to draw themselves toward evil.
From brass they were changed into iron,
So much have they corrupted their conditions;
At which the gods of the halls are joyful—
Halls forever dark and dirty <note>original: "sales"; referring to the gods of the underworld or the infernal regions.</note>—
Who bear envy toward men
As long as they see them alive.

<margin>Note.</margin>
These [gods] have attached in their snares <note>original: "rais"; meaning nets or spokes, here signifying the traps of sin or death.</note>
Those from which they are never torn away:
The sorrowful black sheep,
Weary, wretched, and diseased, <note>original: "morineuses"; afflicted with murrain, a plague of livestock.</note>
Who do not wish to follow the path
That the fair lamb <note>A traditional Christian reference to Jesus Christ as the Lamb of God.</note> presents to them,
By which they would have been entirely free
And their black fleeces <note>original: "toyfons"; meaning the woolly skins or fleeces.</note> made very white,
Had they kept to the great, wide road:
By which they might have come to find shelter there.

### OF THE ROSE

In a company so vast
That it occupied the whole path. <note>Referring to the great number of "black sheep" or sinners who crowd the worldly road.</note>

But never will any beast that goes in there <note>Refers to the fallen, worldly realm previously described as the "Iron Age" or the domain of Jupiter.</note>
Carry a fleece <term>fleece (toyson)</term> of any value,
Nor one from which any cloth could be made,
Except for some horrible hair-shirt <note>original: "haire"; a garment made of coarse animal hair, typically worn by penitents to cause physical discomfort. Here, it symbolizes the spiritual suffering of the wicked.</note>
Which is more sharp and stinging,
When it is pressed against the ribs,
Than would be a fur cloak <note>original: "pelisson"; a luxury garment lined with fur.</note>
Made of shaggy hedgehog skins.
But how much would it be worth to card the wool
Which is so very soft, sweet, and smooth—
Provided that one had such an abundance
To make garments from such a fleece
Which would be taken from the white beasts. <note>The "white sheep" represent the pure of heart or the blessed souls in the celestial garden.</note>
Emperors and kings, and even angels,
Would certainly clothe themselves in it for feasts,
If they were to wear cloths and garments.
Whereby you may well know
That whoever could possess such a robe
Would be most nobly dressed;
And for that very reason
He should hold those sheep more dear,
For there are very few of such beasts.
Nor is the shepherd <note>A reference to the "Good Shepherd" (Christ), who guards the souls of the faithful.</note> foolish
Who guards the flock and the enclosures; <note>original: "lices"; the protective boundaries or palisades of the sacred park.</note>
In this beautiful place—and this is the truth—
He would not let any black beast enter
For anything that one might shout to him.

<summary>This page employs a pastoral allegory to contrast the spiritual condition of the damned and the saved, comparing the prickly "hair-shirts" of the worldly black sheep to the divine, soft wool of the white sheep. It emphasizes that the Good Shepherd strictly guards the entrance to his celestial park, allowing only the pure to enter.</summary>

### XXXVII

### THE ROMANCE

It pleases him so much to select the white ones
That they go to lodge with him;
For they know the shepherd well,
And they are very well known by him,
Whereby they are received all the better.

<margin>Note that all these things are said of paradise.</margin>
I tell you that the most compassionate,
The most beautiful, the most delightful
Of all the worthy animals,
Is the fair and leaping lamb <note>original: "aignel saillant"; a medieval image for the resurrected Christ, who "leaps" with life and vigor.</note>
Who brings the sheep to the park <term>park (parc): the celestial garden or Paradise</term>
Through his labor and through his pain.
For he well knows that if any sheep goes astray,
So that the wolf merely catches sight of her,
The wolf tracks nothing else
Except how to pull her from the path
Of the lamb who intends to lead her;
He [the wolf] will carry her off without defense
And would eat her entirely alive;
Nothing living can protect her from him.
Lords, this lamb awaits us;
But of him we will say no more for now,
Except that we shall pray to God the Father,
That by the intercession of his mother, <note>A reference to the Virgin Mary acting as a mediator for humanity.</note>
He grants those who lead the sheep such good guidance
That the wolves cannot harm them,
And that you do not fail through sin,
So that you may go to play in the park
Which is so beautiful and delightful,
And so lovely with its herbs and flowers.

<summary>This page concludes an allegory where Christ is depicted as a "leaping lamb" leading his flock to the "park" of Paradise, while warning of the wolf (the devil) who preys on those who stray. It ends with a prayer for the spiritual safety of the faithful.</summary>

### CCCLXXVII

## OF THE ROSE

Of violets and of roses,
And of all manner of good things—
If someone were to compare
The beautiful square garden, <note>This refers to the "Garden of Mirth" described at the beginning of the poem, which represents courtly, earthly love.</note>
Enclosed by the small barred gate,
Where that lover <note>The Dreamer, the poem's protagonist.</note> sang the carol, <term>carol (carolle): a popular medieval circle dance accompanied by singing, often associated with courtly festivities.</term>
Or where Mirth and his people dance—
If one wished to compare that place
To this beautiful park that I describe,
Which is so precious beyond measure,
He would commit too great a mistake;
He would find it as ill-matched
As one would find the truth compared to a fable.
For whoever might be inside this park,
Or who merely cast an eye within,
Would surely dare to judge
That the other garden would be as nothing

<margin>All the pleasures of the world are not to be compared to the joys of paradise.</margin>

In comparison to this enclosure,
Which is not made in a square shape,
But is so round and so exquisite
That never was there a beryl stone or a city
Of a form so perfectly rounded. <note>The square shape of the earthly garden represents the four corners of the material world, whereas the circle of the celestial park represents the perfection and infinity of God.</note>
What more would you have me say?
Let us speak of the things seen then,
Both inside and outside;
And let us pass over them in brief words,
So that we do not grow too weary.
From there, he saw the little images <term>little images (ymaigettes): small sculpted or painted figures, likely referring to the personifications of vices found on the exterior walls of the garden.</term>
Portrayed on the wall outside the garden;
But whoever searched outside this park
Would find every kind of figure there.

It notes that the heavenly park is perfectly circular, contrasting it with the square shape of the earthly garden.</summary>

<margin>Note.</margin>
Hell with all the devils,
Most hideous and most terrifying,
And all the faults and all the outrages
Who make their dwelling in hell; <note>The poem suggests that vices and sins are "hostages" or residents of hell, forever imprisoned there.</note>
And Cerberus who chains all things, <term>Cerberus: In classical mythology, the three-headed dog guarding the entrance to the underworld; here used as an allegorical figure of hell’s power to imprison.</term>

And the fire that surrounds all else, <note>According to the medieval "four elements" theory, the sphere of fire was the outermost layer of the elemental world, sitting just below the heavens.</note>
The contents and the holdings
Of all the other elements.
He would see all the stars
In clear and beautiful splendor,
Whether wandering <term>wandering (errans): a reference to the planets, which move across the sky, as opposed to the "fixed" stars.</term> or fixed,
Attached within their own spheres.
Whoever was there would see all these things
Excluded from this beautiful park, <note>This is a structural parallel to the beginning of the poem. Drawn there as clearly
As if they were actually made visible.
¶ Now let us go into the garden,
And speak of the things within.

It establishes a mirror image of the poem's opening, where the earthly garden also featured exterior depictions of things that could not enter.</summary>

Everyone will do their penance there,
