Some will come there secretly,
And others quite openly.
But those who come in secret
Will be held as upright men, <note>original: "preudhommes." In the medieval social code, a man's reputation often depended more on his discretion than his actual behavior.</note>
While the others will be defamed
And called ribald brothel-goers,
Even though they are no more to blame
Than those whom no one accuses.
Now, it is true that some wicked men—
Whom may God and the Holy Father of Rome <note>A reference to the Pope.</note>
Confound, along with their business—
Will leave the roses to do far worse; <note>Venus is referring to those who reject natural procreation (the "roses") in favor of what the poem considers "unnatural" vices or sodomy.</note>
And the devils who urge them on
Shall give them a crown of nettles.
<margin>Genius is the god of generation, to be properly understood.</margin>
For Genius, <note>In the Roman de la Rose, Genius is the priest of Mother Nature; he represents the drive to procreate and ensures the survival of the species.</note> acting for Nature,
Because of their vice and their filth,
Has placed them all under sentence
Along with our other enemies.
Shame, if I do not outwit you,
Then my art and skill are worth little,
And I shall never call myself [Venus];
Certainly, I shall not love you,
Nor you, nor Reason your mother,
Who is so bitter to lovers.
Whoever believed you or your mother
Would never, I believe, have any joy."
Venus intended to say no more,
For this was enough for her.

<summary>Venus declares that she will open the Rose to all, though she distinguishes between those who love discreetly and those who are shamed. She specifically condemns those who reject procreation (natural love) and insults Shame and her mother, Reason.</summary>

CCCLXXXVI

### OF THE ROSE

aa ii

Venus then girded herself up,
Appearing very much like a woman in a rage.
She draws her bow and notches her torch; <note>Venus traditionally carries a "brandon" or torch, representing the fire of passion, which she uses here as an arrow.</note>
When the string was set in the notch,
She draws the bow back to her ear,
A bow no longer than a *toise*. <term>toise: a medieval unit of measurement roughly equal to six feet or a fathom.</term>
Then, like a skilled archeress,
Through a very small embrasure <note>original: "archiere." In this architectural allegory, the "arrow-slit" or embrasure refers to the lady's anatomy.</note>
Which she saw set in the tower—
At the front, not on the side—
Which Nature, with great mastery,
Had placed between two beautiful pillars.
The beautiful pillars were made of ivory,
Very elegant, and they supported silver.
In place of a shrine, there was a beautiful image, <note>In the medieval context, a "chasse" was a reliquary or shrine for a saint. The poet is using religious architecture to describe the beloved's body.</note>
Which was neither too high nor too low,
Neither too stout nor too slender,
But perfectly proportioned
In arms, shoulders, and hands,
So that nothing was lacking, more or less.
The other limbs were very elegant,
And smelled sweeter than ambergris apples. <note>original: "pōmes dambres." These were pomanders—perforated balls containing perfumes like ambergris, musk, or civet, often carried to provide a pleasant scent.</note>
Inside was a sanctuary,
Covered with a precious shroud, <note>original: "suaire." While this can mean a burial cloth, here it refers to a fine, decorative fabric or veil protecting the "holy" site of the Rose.</note>
The most noble and the finest
To be found as far as Constantinople.
And if anyone using reason
Wished to make a comparison
Of this image to any other well-crafted portrait,
They would find its equal in this one.

What Pygmalion did long ago
Like a cat facing a lion <note>A proverbial expression of the time suggesting a bold transformation or a small thing attempting a great, perhaps impossible, feat.</note>

### ¶ Here begins the story
### Of the image of Pygmalion

Pygmalion was a sculptor <term>entailleur: a carver or sculptor who works in various media.</term>
Fashioning the finest work in iron,
And likewise in stones,
In wood and with other tools,
In metals, in bone, and in wax,
And in all other materials
That can be used for such work.
And to put his skill <term>engin: innate talent, ingenuity, or technical craft.</term> to the test,
And also to delight himself,
He made an image of ivory.
He put such great care into its making
That it was so pleasing and noble
That it seemed to be as alive
As the most beautiful living thing.
Never were Helen or Lavinia <note>Helen of Troy and Lavinia, the wife of Aeneas, were the two most famous standards of female beauty in medieval literature.</note>
Of such a fine complexion,
Nor born with such beautiful features—
However well-fashioned they might have been—
They did not have even a tenth of her beauty.
All his senses were overwhelmed by it
As he looked at it more and more;
And he, who was not on his guard,
Love entangled him in his reeds, <note>original: "roseaux." A metaphor for the snares or traps set by the god of Love, often depicted as a thicket or marshy area where one gets stuck.</note>
So that he knows not what to do.

And to himself he makes his complaint,
But he cannot staunch his grief;
"Alas! What am I doing?" he says, "Am I dreaming?
Many an image have I made and forged,
Whose value no one could ever name, <note>Literally: "one knew not how to say their price," implying they were of inestimable worth.</note>
Yet I was never overtaken by love for them.
Now, by this one, I am brought to a wretched state;
Because of her, all my reason has failed me.
Alas! From where does this thought come to me?
Where was it found or conceived?

I love an image deaf and mute,
Who neither stirs nor moves,
And who will never have mercy <term>mercy: in the tradition of courtly love, "mercy" or "pity" is the favor granted by a lady to her lover.</term> on me.
How will such a love wound me?
For there is no one who might hear of it
Who would not be completely astonished.
Now I am the greatest fool in the world, <term>sicle: from the Latin "saeculum," referring here to the world or the present age.</term>
What can I do in this situation?
For if I loved some queen,
I might still hope for mercy,
Because that is a possible thing;
But this love is too horrible,
For it does not come from Nature. <note>Nature is personified here as the creative force of the universe; Pygmalion feels his desire for an inanimate object violates the natural order.</note>
Too poorly do I behave against my own nature;
Nature has a bad son in me.
In this she greatly erred— <note>original: "forment sauilla." This suggests Nature made a mistake or debased herself in her creation of him.</note>
Yet I must not blame her;
If I choose to love so foolishly,
I must blame no one but myself,
Since Pygmalion is my name."

### THE ROMANCE OF

Ever since I first could walk on my own two feet,
I have never heard tell of such a love;
<margin>Note.</margin> And yet, I do not love too foolishly,
For if the written word does not lie,
Many have loved far more foolishly.
Did not Narcissus, in the leafy woods,
Beside the fountain clear and pure,
Fall in love with his own reflection? <note>Narcissus is a figure from Greek mythology who fell in love with his own image in a pool of water and wasted away because he could not possess it.</note>
When he thought to quench his thirst,
He could never more recover from it,
But died of it, according to the story
Which is still well-remembered today.
Thus, I am nonetheless less of a fool,
For whenever I wish, I go to her,
And I take her, embrace her, and kiss her,
By which I can better endure my distress.
But that man could never have the one
Whom he saw within the little spring.
Furthermore, in many different lands,
Many lovers have loved their ladies,
And served them as best they could,
And never received even a single kiss;
So they suffered most grievously.
Has Love then dealt with me better?
No, they have it better; for despite their doubts,
They still possess a sense of hope
For kisses and for other things, <note>original: "aultre chose." A common medieval euphemism for sexual intimacy.</note>
Of which hope is not entirely shut out,
Regarding the delight awaited by those
Who seek the pleasures of love.

For when I wish to cling to her,

As a stake and just as cold;

She turns my whole mouth cold.
Ah! I have spoken far too foolishly!
I beg for mercy, sweet lady,
And pray that you accept my penance, <note>original: "lamende." In the tradition of courtly love, a lover must often offer "amende" (reparations or penance) for a perceived slight or "folly" against his lady or the God of Love.</note>
For so long as you deign
To look sweetly and laugh upon me,
That should be quite enough for me;
For sweet looks and pitying smiles
Are most delightful to lovers.

Pygmalion then falls to his knees,

But she cares nothing for his penance,
For she neither hears nor feels
A thing of him or of his offerings,
So that he fears his labor is all in vain—
He who strives to love such a thing.
Yet he knows not how to reclaim his heart,
For Love <note>original: "amours." In this poem, Love is often personified as a powerful and sometimes cruel god who strips his followers of their rational mind.</note> strips away all sense and reason.

"And here I become yours, and you mine;

Then he sings with a high, clear voice
Songs full of great merriment,
In place of masses, he sings little ditties
About the pretty secrets of young lovers;
And he makes his instruments sound
So loudly that one cannot hear God thundering.
For he had very many kinds of them,
Both better and more complete
Than **Amphion of Thebes** <note>In Greek mythology, Amphion was a son of Zeus whose magical playing of the lyre moved stones to build the walls of the city of Thebes.</note> ever possessed.

With wheels made very skillfully
In perpetual motion.
He had organs that were very easy to handle,
Portable with a single hand <note>original: "orgues... a une seule main portables." Known as a portative organ, this small pipe organ was strapped to the player, who pumped the bellows with one hand and played the keys with the other.</note>,

**Motets** <note>term: "mottetz" / motets. A complex form of polyphonic choral music popular in the 13th and 14th centuries.</note> in counterpoint and tenor;

Then he takes his panpipes <note>original: "freteaulx."</note> and plays a refrain.

The flower from the beautiful leafy rosebush;
Thus I had the vermilion rose.
At that moment, it was day, and I awoke. <note>This marks the end of the "dream frame," a popular medieval literary device where the entire narrative is revealed to be a vision experienced by the narrator while asleep.</note>

¶ The end of the Romance of the Rose, reviewed and corrected beyond previous printings. And printed in Paris, by master Pierre Vidoue, for Galliot du Pré, sworn bookseller <term>libraire juré: a bookseller officially licensed and sworn in by the University of Paris</term>, keeping his shop at the Palace <note>The Palais de Justice in Paris was the center of the legal and social world, where prominent booksellers like Du Pré rented stalls around the pillars of the Great Hall.</note>, at the first pillar. In the month of March, one thousand five hundred twenty-nine, before Easter <note>original: "avant pasques." At this time in France, the new year began on Easter Sunday rather than January 1st. Therefore, "March 1529 before Easter" actually falls in the year 1530 by our modern calendar.</note>.

<summary>The poem concludes with the Dreamer finally plucking the Rose and waking from his long vision. This is followed by a printer's colophon identifying the book as a 1529 edition by the famous Parisian publisher Galliot du Pré.</summary>
